usd3-3jane.title: Senior Credit Is Still Credit
usd3-3jane.text: USD3 packages 3Jane's senior credit tranche into an ERC-4626 share: USDC enters, idle cash waits in Aave, and the rest finances fintech receivables and crypto credit lines. Its NAV can rise above a dollar because interest accrues into the share price, so the familiar ticker is doing fund accounting rather than promising a fixed $1 quote. sUSD3 absorbs losses first, but that protection is only as thick as the junior tranche, and recoveries from an impaired off-chain borrower can take months or years. Backing is the weakest of the three pillars behind the {{grade}} overall grade, and the reason is plain: the credit receivables, roughly nine-tenths of the book at the last on-chain capture, are scored as receivables rather than folded into the dollar they settle in, so the liquid Aave buffer and the deployed book are priced apart instead of averaged into a comfortable middle. That separation is the whole point, because the buffer, the exit route, and the unit of account are all the same dollar. A haircut upstream would reach every part of the structure at once. The senior seat is safer than the junior one; it is still a claim on 3Jane's credit book, not on the dollar it settles in.

kusd-kerne.title: Base synthetic dollar with USDC PSM
kusd-kerne.text: kUSD is Kerne Protocol's Base-native synthetic dollar. A first external audit from Hexens landed in late July with zero criticals and every finding confined to the yield vault. The audit followed a patched Peg Stability Module cutover that opened permissionless 1:1 USDC minting. Circulating supply remains at genesis scale. DefiLlama indexes the supply with no usable price, and CoinGecko still does not resolve the coin, so Pharos keeps it on the upcoming tracker. The live KerneVault still runs pre-audit bytecode with deposits closed until the remediated version deploys, so the audited code and the deployed code are not yet the same thing. Current backing is USDC in the PSM contracts, covering outstanding kUSD slightly above 1:1. The ambitious delta-neutral design, using a WETH vault and Hyperliquid short, remains degraded and excluded from reserves. Since August 6, kUSD role administration and PSM configuration sit behind a 48-hour timelock whose sole proposer and executor is a 2-of-3 Safe, and hourly signed proof-of-reserves is published at kerne.fi/verify. The durable constraint is distribution: the protocol keeps shipping before users arrive.

usdt-tether.title: Treasury-Heavy Dollar Base
usdt-tether.text: USDT's {{grade}} overall grade is the sound of scale winning arguments: the peg record and the exit pillar sit at the top of the scale, economic control is strong, and backing is the weakest of the three pillars. That backing line carries secured loans, gold, bitcoin, and equities alongside the {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} wall, and the card flags the attested composition as older than v9's freshness bound between quarterly reports. The Q2 2026 BDO attestation keeps assets ahead of liabilities, but the excess reserve buffer nearly halved in a single quarter to roughly $4 billion, a thin cushion against a book of well over $180 billion that gold marks and bitcoin swings flow through. USDT0 extends the franchise across another wave of chains through lock-and-mint rails, useful for distribution and a reminder that omnichain convenience is not the same thing as issuer decentralization. The {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} floor is real for eligible Tether customers, but it remains governed by Tether's terms, discretion, and quarterly {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} cadence rather than continuous bank-style disclosure. The freeze surface is verified at the contract level: the Ethereum token exposes owner-only blacklist, fund-destruction, and pause functions, and Tether's terms reserve the right to use them. In Europe the MiCA wall keeps rising, with Revolut's announced delisting of USDT for EU users at the end of August 2026 and forced conversion of whatever remained. The canonical lesson stands: the biggest stablecoin can be operationally serious and structurally centralized at the same time.

sources.label: CoinDesk: Tether Q2 2026 attestation ($1.5B operating profit, reserve buffer falls by half)
CoinUnited: Revolut delists USDT for EU users by August 31, 2026 under MiCA

usdc-circle.title: The Institutional Default
usdc-circle.text: USDC is crypto's compliance-first reserve currency: cash and cash equivalents sit in the Circle Reserve Fund, managed by BlackRock and custodied at BNY Mellon, while monthly Deloitte examinations reconcile assets and liabilities. The curated composition is anchored to the June 30 examination and Circle's live transparency feed still resolves cleanly against it. Short-dated Treasuries carry most of the weight, with overnight reverse repo and bank deposits split by systemic importance underneath. Its on-chain liquidity is unusually distributed, so a dollar that exits one venue does not have to leave the market altogether, and the SVB weekend remains the reminder that banking access can still interrupt an otherwise conservative reserve stack. The {{grade}} overall grade is doing a narrow job: it says the reserve and the exit are about as good as this asset class gets, while the ordinary weakness remains. That weakness is still the point of centralization: direct {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} runs through Circle, and Circle can control the token. USDC is intentionally boring infrastructure, provided the gatekeeper and its bank-and-fund chain remain boring too.

dai-makerdao.title: The OG Decentralized Dollar
dai-makerdao.text: DAI is MakerDAO's decentralized USD stablecoin, the one that proved crypto could create a dollar without a bank account: {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-minted origins, now mostly backed by PSM stablecoins and Sky's allocator books. The {{grade}} report card still rests on genuine DAO governance rather than a multisig cosplaying as one, though the economic-control pillar is the weakest of the three, a reminder that even the OG DAO keeps levers someone can pull. The reserve composition has drifted far from crypto-purist origins: roughly two-fifths other stablecoins through the {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}}, Grove's institutional-credit and Spark's lending allocations near a quarter each, and only a single-digit sliver left in the crypto vaults that made DAI famous. It is functionally a hybrid fiat-credit dollar. The peg record is strong over four years of tracking, and the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop, powered by atomic PSM access at zero fee, earns an exit pillar at the top of the scale, more than almost anything else on the dashboard can claim. Now overshadowed by its own rebrand as USDS, DAI occupies a strange position: still billions in circulation, the philosophical North Star of decentralized money, increasingly backed by the centralized assets it was designed to replace. CDP vaults remain the original minting path.

frax-frax.title: From Algorithm to T-Bill Basket
frax-frax.text: FRAX abandoned its {{term:algorithmic}}fractional-algorithmic{{/term}} origins to become a tokenized {{term:treasury}}T-bill{{/term}} basket, and the balance sheet now leans on WisdomTree WTGXX, Superstate USTB, BlackRock BUIDL, and a small Ethena strategy sleeve alongside a large block of Frax-owned FRAX, frxUSD, and sFRAX liquidity. That last block is the problem the report card keeps flagging: backing is the weakest of the three pillars, with a sizeable share of the reserve in the protocol's own paper and an issuer that publishes self-reported USD values with no independent NAV reconciliation for legacy FRAX. The {{grade}} overall grade sits beside a peg history with a long tail of episodes across more than three years of tracking, a token still prone to drift below par, and stress monitoring that has not stayed at the calm end of the scale. FRAX sits in an uncomfortable middle, too decentralized-dependent for institutional comfort and too TradFi-backed for DeFi purists, while Frax's own frxUSD now sits inside the reserve as its successor. The durable constraint is circularity: a legacy dollar partly backed by its own successor and its own liquidity cannot be graded on the T-bills alone.

tusd-trueusd.title: Daily Attestation, Illiquid Reserve
tusd-trueusd.text: TrueUSD is Techteryx's dollar stablecoin, and its paperwork is unusually frequent: Moore CPA signs a reasonable-assurance report on the reserve every day. What those reports disclose is the problem. Effectively the entire reserve sits at cost in a single First Digital Trust fund position, in instruments the attestor's own notes say cannot be readily converted to cash, against a backdrop of redemption litigation and a DIFC worldwide freezing order of up to $456 million. The reserve total still exceeds tokens issued, and most of the supply is held by Techteryx itself rather than the public float. Archblock's Chapter 11 filing, Kraken's delisting, and S&P's weakest stablecoin stability score sit in the notices. On the card, backing scores in the upper half because the attestation and reconciliation are strong even where the asset is illiquid, while exit is the weakest of the three pillars, with {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} running through a single issuer. The peg itself has held near par for over a year. A daily {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} of a reserve you cannot get out of is the most precisely measured illiquidity in the asset class, and the {{grade}} overall grade describes a product that survives on institutional inertia rather than anything the name still promises.

sources.label: Moore CPA Independent Assurance Report on the TUSD Consolidated Reserves Report - August 7, 2026

lusd-liquity.title: The Immutable Benchmark
lusd-liquity.text: LUSD remains the philosophical standard for decentralized stablecoins: ETH-only collateral, immutable contracts, no admin keys, no governance, no upstream dependencies. The design earns near-perfect marks on the exit and economic-control pillars, while the same ETH-only purity keeps backing a notch lower and holds the overall grade at {{grade}}, short of what its reputation implies. The permissionless {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop is the load-bearing piece, providing a hard floor at $1 by letting anyone swap LUSD for $1 of ETH from the riskiest Trove in exchange for 50 bps. The hundreds of recorded peg deviations reveal the trade-off of purity rather than weakness: ETH-only backing at 110% minimum pushes borrowers to hold safety margins, producing persistent above-peg drift, and every ETH crash tests the Stability Pool's absorption capacity in real time. Supply keeps slowly bleeding, down more than an order of magnitude from its 2021-era peak. This is the fate of a v1 protocol overshadowed by its own successor BOLD, which added multi-collateral support and user-set interest rates. LUSD is increasingly a monument rather than a market participant. It is the stablecoin that proved decentralization works and then watched the market choose convenience anyway.

mim-abracadabra.title: Battle-Scarred CDP at a Deep Discount
mim-abracadabra.text: Battle-scarred {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin minted against Abracadabra cauldrons; reflexive peg, no modeled {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop, and a remaining user base too stubborn or leveraged to leave. Magic Internet Money has survived multiple cauldron exploits, a treasury-manager scandal, a governance token collapse, and a long history of violent peg excursions, which makes its continued existence less a triumph than a lab result. The collateral base still reads like a museum of DeFi exotica: yvDAI dominates, WBTC is material, and smaller yvWETH/WETH cauldrons keep the wrapper risk alive. The mechanism is reflexive rather than structural. Borrowers buy discounted MIM to repay debt, which only works when borrowers exist and care about their positions. June finally broke the pattern: MIM crashed through half a dollar in its worst depeg on record, Abracadabra's emergency response, including rate hikes, incentive pauses, and a token Curve-pool injection, failed to hold the line, and Pharos's multi-source feed now prices the token at a deep double-digit discount with the report card at F. MIM earned its cockroach reputation by surviving what killed everything else; this time the exterminator appears to be arithmetic.

usdp-paxos.title: The Credentialed Reference Implementation
usdp-paxos.text: Paxos's USDP is backed by very-low-risk reserves split across short-dated {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}, overnight repos, and FDIC-insured cash, attested monthly by KPMG under Paxos's OCC National Trust Charter. Backing and economic control are the product's obvious strengths in the Safety Score V9 report card; the gap between those pillars and a genuinely elite overall grade lives in the exit pillar, because thin markets remain the asset's perennial soft spot. USDP has become less a growth product than a credentialed reference implementation. Paxos's real business is white-labeling stablecoin infrastructure for PayPal, Global Dollar Network, and formerly Binance. The depeg events on record read like thin-market artifacts rather than backing failure, but thin markets are still what holders have to trade through. The current package remains one of the cleaner compliance-to-reserves stories in the small-cap tier, with zero-fee {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} as the structural floor under a token almost nobody seems eager to hold.

usdd-tron-dao-reserve.title: Back to TRX-Heavy Backing
usdd-tron-dao-reserve.text: USDD has pivoted again: the reserve is once more dominated by TRX as CDP collateral, with a sliver of sTRX, alongside a Smart Allocator sleeve of DeFi strategies and a thin USDT PSM buffer, a return to the TRX-heavy {{term:algorithmic}}volatile-asset{{/term}} composition that defined USDD's earlier era. That is a striking backing profile for an asset that now carries a {{grade}} overall grade, dragged down by a failing economic-control pillar, the weakest of the three, and the structural fact that its dollar value rests on the most volatile single asset in the TRON orbit. The peg itself behaves better than the rest of the profile deserves, but that surface stability has been bought across hundreds of brief deviations over the years. The {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} backstop remains the load-bearing piece: permissionless atomic swaps with zero fees and an immediate USDT exit lane give the exit pillar a redemption quality the surrounding reserve mix can't match. With Dominica jurisdiction and governance still set by fiat, USDD survives not on collateral merit but on the TRON ecosystem's captive demand and its founder's conviction that centralized control is a feature.

dola-inverse-finance.title: Rebuilt on FiRM, Concentrated in sUSDe
dola-inverse-finance.text: DOLA is Inverse Finance's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-style stablecoin minted through FiRM's fixed-rate lending markets, with a USDS {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} as its peg floor. The April 2022 oracle-manipulation exploit that let an attacker borrow DOLA against manipulated collateral left scars that became load-bearing, and the protocol rebuilt on FiRM's organic borrower demand rather than token emissions. The collateral base has become anything but diversified: sUSDe makes up roughly four-fifths of the backing, with sUSDS most of the rest, a concentration that effectively chains DOLA's fate to Ethena's synthetic dollar even though the backing pillar grades between the other two. The {{grade}} overall grade is instead set by the exit pillar, the weakest of the three, where the PSM backstop is real but thin against the peg history: hundreds of brief sub-peg blips and a worst deviation that once approached total collapse remain the asterisk on every metric. The sDOLA {{term:yield-bearing}}yield{{/term}} remains the quiet attraction, sourced from actual borrower interest, and supply changes require an INV vote plus a 48-hour timelock, which is why economic control holds up. The Fantom and BSC representations still carry a holder-burn primitive with no minter delay. DOLA is minted from overcollateralized FiRM loans with {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} backstops, and its central trade-off is that those backstops now sit downstream of one issuer.

sdola-inverse-finance.title: DOLA With an Exchange Rate
sdola-inverse-finance.text: sDOLA is the ERC-4626 wrapper around DOLA's savings account, which means the stablecoin risk is still DOLA and the extra product risk is the exchange-rate wrapper sitting on top. FiRM borrowing revenue is converted through the DBR-DOLA auction and compounded into a rising DOLA:sDOLA exchange rate, so the yield is tied to borrower demand rather than token emissions. The wrapper does not create new base DOLA supply, but holders still inherit DOLA's CDP collateral mix, governance, and any upstream stress in the parent peg. Cross-chain deployments on Base, Optimism, Arbitrum, and Berachain are Chainlink CCIP burn-mint representations with Ethereum as the source of truth, so the bridge path is part of the exit math on those chains. The {{grade}} overall grade is capped at the parent DOLA rating.

gusd-gemini.title: Pristine Reserves, Thin Liquidity
gusd-gemini.text: GUSD is Gemini Trust's NYDFS-chartered dollar, redeemable 1:1 through Gemini against reserves that the May 2026 BPM examination reported as cash deposits at State Street and Western Alliance Bank, held in segregated accounts for holders. It has pristine compliance and almost no users. The {{grade}} overall grade renders that split plainly: backing and economic control are the strong pillars, while the exit pillar is the weakest line on the card because on-chain exit remains a mostly theoretical exercise. With circulating supply down more than 90% from its late-2022 peak, GUSD has become a regulated product few people hold. Its long tail of brief price blips is the signature of an asset so thinly traded that any flow nudges the quote, with the sharpest excursions skewing negative even as the peg recovers each time. Mint authority is bounded: a limited-printer key can issue under a 1.36 billion GUSD ceiling, and raising it takes a 2-of-3 custodian plus a one-hour delay. Gemini built the compliance-first stablecoin that regulators asked for; the durable constraint is that almost nobody trades it.

sources.label: DefiLlama: Gemini Dollar circulating supply history

alusd-alchemix.title: Self-Repaying Dollar
alusd-alchemix.text: alUSD is Alchemix's self-repaying {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin: deposit DAI, USDC, or USDT into Yearn and Aave yield strategies, borrow up to roughly 50% against it, and let the yield slowly erase your debt with no interest and no {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} risk. The mechanism remains DeFi's most patient financial product, and the Transmuter still backstops 1:1 {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} on a queue that settles over days. But the elegance has a price the report card spells out plainly: a {{grade}} overall grade, driven by a peg record so poor that the v9 peg multiplier does most of the damage; self-repaying loans strip out the debt-repayment urgency that normally generates buying pressure to defend the peg. The peg has logged brief deviations by the hundreds across its history, so holders are effectively trading away peg discipline for the no-liquidation feature. Exit routes are thin, backing is held back because the card admits no current reserve composition, and economic control is now the weakest of the three pillars: local token admins can re-authorize the Alchemist or raise mint ceilings, and the proxy paths remain mutable. A stress-prone instrument that only makes sense if you value never being liquidated above all else.

susd-synthetix.title: Retired Below Par
susd-synthetix.text: Synthetix's sUSD is no longer the simple SNX debt-pool dollar older DeFi muscle memory remembers. The current reserve story is split across legacy SNX exposure, V3 USDC/stataUSDC collateral, ETH/LST collateral, and protocol treasury or SLP-vault activity, which is a long way of saying the peg now depends on governance executing a cleanup plan. Pharos flags the prolonged discount because this is not a theoretical stress test; the token has been living below its target while the V3 transition and basis-trade restoration plan try to rebuild demand. The mint path is governed through Synthetix admin control rather than immutable borrower autonomy, so holders are underwriting both collateral volatility and political patience. In June the roadmap ran out: governance passed SIP-423, retiring sUSD outright. The contract is frozen. Holders are compensated at four SNX per sUSD on a year's lock and a year's vest. Pharos no longer gets a continuous price read on what was DeFi's original synthetic dollar. Eight years of peg engineering ends not with a bang but with a conversion schedule.

ousd-origin-protocol.title: The Passive Yield Play
ousd-origin-protocol.text: Origin Dollar is a {{term:yield-bearing}}rebasing{{/term}} USDC wrapper: deposits are minted 1:1 into the OUSD Vault, which deploys the USDC into Morpho lending and Curve {{term:amo}}AMO{{/term}} liquidity, and opted-in balances grow daily without staking or locking. Smart contracts must explicitly opt in to receive yield, so OUSD sitting in non-opted AMM pools transfers its attributable return to opted-in balances. Permissionless atomic stablecoin {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} at a small fee provides a structural floor that a long tail of brief depeg episodes has tested but not broken. The {{grade}} overall grade is held back by the backing pillar, the weakest of the three: the collateral is USDC, but it sits in protocol positions whose strategy weights Origin does not publish, and the Vault retains a privileged burn path over holder balances. That is what the exotic collateral quality and wrapper governance classification describe: a USDC yield strategy with a rebasing token wrapper rather than an independent stablecoin with its own reserve management. It is a well-engineered product for the small cohort that wants DeFi yield without the DeFi homework.

cusd-celo.title: Stablecoins All the Way Down
cusd-celo.text: Mento Dollar (USDm, formerly cUSD) is Mento's oracle-priced dollar on Celo, and its reserve is an exercise in recursive stablecoin nesting: roughly three-quarters of the book is other people's stablecoins, with AUSD and sUSDS the largest slices and USDT, EUROP, EURC, and USDC layered on top, so most of USDm's backing is itself backed elsewhere, each layer with its own dependency chain and failure modes. A long tail of mostly minor depeg events and a double-digit worst drawdown are hard numbers to look past. The {{grade}} overall grade is set by the exit pillar, the weakest of the three, while backing holds up comparatively well: {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} runs through Mento reserve swaps rather than fiat off-ramps, Pharos has no comparable same-notional route to score, and the on-chain depth behind those swaps is thin. Economic control sits between the two: the Mento Safe that owns the Celo token can authorise a burner able to destroy any holder balance and can replace the implementation immediately. The thesis remains phone-number wallets in places like Nairobi rather than DeFi composability on Ethereum. The CELO allocation, roughly a fifth of the reserve, is the wildcard in an otherwise stablecoin-heavy book: the one asset that can crater in a downturn precisely when a thin {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} buffer matters most.

eurc-circle.title: MiCA's Compliance Moat
eurc-circle.text: Circle's EURC is the regulatory standard-bearer for euro stablecoins: an ACPR-licensed EMI under MiCA, {{term:attestation}}Deloitte-examined{{/term}} monthly, and now live on roughly a dozen chains rather than the handful it launched with. The June 30 examination shows a reserve that is entirely cash at regulated financial institutions: no securities whatsoever, which is defensible for a euro float and a reminder that EURC's real counterparty is a set of banks Circle declines to name, with only a sliver of the balance sitting where the feed marks the institution as systemically important. The {{grade}} overall grade carries that examination: backing and economic control sit close together, and exit liquidity is the strongest line on the card. EURC's float is still small next to USDC, and a pool that thin registers tremors a deeper one would never feel, even when the stress panel reads quiet; the peg record shows a handful of episodes across four years of tracking, none of them recent.

eurs-stasis.title: STASIS Euro's Drifting Quote
eurs-stasis.text: EURS is STASIS's euro stablecoin, launched in 2018 as the first of its category and redeemable 1:1 through STSS (Malta) Limited against euro balances at licensed EU institutions. The current transparency page allocates the entire reserve to a Lietuvos bankas account reached through NexPay UAB, updated daily but self-published, with no independent {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} and no disclosed account agreement or segregation terms, which holds backing to the middle of the range on a card where all three pillars cluster together. The {{grade}} overall grade sits well below any of the pillars, and the peg record is the reason on view: EURS has logged dozens of depeg episodes across four years of tracking, on both sides of par, including an April 2026 whipsaw and a worst logged deviation above a third of par, and the peg score is the weakest line on the card. A quote that thin is a market-structure problem more than a reserve problem: {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} at a central-bank account can keep the claim whole while the traded price wanders. Distribution spans seven chains, three of them third-party lock-and-mint representations including a Multichain route on Arbitrum, and the token is recorded as MiCA non-compliant. With no depth to exit into, the quote is whatever the last thin trade says it is.

sources.label: Blockchain Magazine on the April 2026 EURS depeg swing

ceur-celo.title: Mento's Reserve-Backed Euro
ceur-celo.text: EURm, formerly cEUR, is Mento's oracle-priced euro stablecoin on Celo, minted and redeemed against the shared Mento Reserve through Fixed-Price Market Maker pools that quote a Chainlink EUR rate rather than deriving price from pool depth, with circuit breakers halting trade when the feed is stale or off-peg. The reserve is a diversified basket led by AUSD and sUSDS, with CELO, USDT, EURC, USDC, stETH, and ETH behind them, {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} under a stable-asset mandate but still crypto-backed, so EURm inherits both on-chain transparency and the volatility of that mix. Those reserve swaps are the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} route, and the exit pillar is the strongest line on the {{grade}} card. Economic control is the weakest: the Mento Broker is a live burner that can burn from any holder balance, the owner Safe can add burners or operators, and a Wormhole NTT route carries a material share of supply to Monad, while residual Ethereum, Polygon, and Solana balances are legacy bridged cEUR. The peg record is the caution flag: Pharos has logged a long tail of deviation episodes, including one extreme print, and the price feed carries low confidence because trading is thin. In the euro stablecoin race dominated by Circle's EURC and MiCA-licensed competitors, EURm's niche is geographic rather than regulatory, and it is not MiCA-compliant.

fpi-frax.title: CPI on a Blockchain
fpi-frax.text: FPI is Frax's CPI-tracking stablecoin backed by FRAX reserves and {{term:amo}}AMO{{/term}}-generated yield, with a {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} price that ratchets upward every second at the trailing 12-month CPI-U rate via a Chainlink oracle. That makes it both a stablecoin and an inflation derivative with a single-issuer dependency: exactly the recursive exposure the report card flags as the soft spot, with backing the weakest of the three pillars, since FPI's collateral quality is only as good as FRAX itself and the chain inherits every flaw upstream carries. The rest of the card is firmer, with exit and economic control both grading ahead of backing to hold a {{grade}} overall. The durable constraint is upstream: whatever weakens legacy FRAX flows straight into FPI's backing.

uusd-youves.title: Tezos CDP With No Market Left
uusd-youves.text: Youves's uUSD is a Tezos {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} backed overwhelmingly by USDt, with residual XTZ, tzBTC, and SIRS LP tokens, and its report card carries a {{grade}} overall grade with a Safety Score of {{score}} out of 100. The peg failure is long-running and still flagged active. It has years of recorded depeg events, zero DEX pools, no backstop route, and no market mechanism left to enforce parity on a Tezos ecosystem that emptied out beneath it. The one dark joke in the report card is that backing is its best pillar: the {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} vault math still technically works, which counts for little when exit and control sit at the floor. And the rigor mortis has finally broken. Circulating value roughly halved from the plateau it held into early July 2026, less stability now than slow-motion dismantling as remaining vault owners unwind what markets no longer price. The uUSD story remains a cautionary tale about chain risk: sound {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} mechanics are worthless when the entire ecosystem around them goes dark.

lisusd-lista.title: BNB Chain's CDP Bet
lisusd-lista.text: Lista DAO's lisUSD transplants the MakerDAO {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} playbook to BNB Chain, with a {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} accepting USDT, USDC, and FDUSD for peg stability. The collateral book is far more concentrated than the multi-asset design implies: at the September census, slisBNB, Lista's own liquid-staking token, made up almost the entire priced GemJoin collateral, with BTCB and wBETH as small remainders and the remaining markets at dust levels. Pharos withdrew the live reserve feed because the adapter could not value every positive branch exactly, so backing is scored on a curated, selected-slice basis with limited evidence. The peg record shows a long tail of depeg episodes over four years of tracking, including one collapse of more than half its value, making lisUSD one of the most frequently depegged CDPs at scale. Economic control is the weakest pillar on the card because effective minting is scored as unbounded. The exit pillar also fails: its routes were measured under different stress requests, and no comparable same-notional exit route is compiled. Deployed only on BSC with alt-LST collateral quality and no jurisdiction or proof of reserves disclosed, lisUSD's safety profile depends on BNB's price stability, slisBNB's liquidity, and the PSM's capacity to absorb redemption pressure. Whether lisUSD can grow beyond Binance-subsidized adoption remains the central question for a CDP whose collateral and distribution both flow through a single ecosystem, with BNB-heavy {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} and LST-collateral {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} risk as the structural constraint.

eure-monerium.title: SEPA Native, DeFi Adopted
eure-monerium.text: EURE is Monerium's MiCA-regulated euro e-money, minted and burned against SEPA transfers, with the bulk of reserves safeguarded in State Street's AAA-rated EUR LVNAV {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market fund{{/term}} and the rest in deposits at Arion and LHV, at weights Monerium does not publish. The SEPA-to-IBAN integration lets users move between euros and on-chain tokens without the friction that plagues most stablecoin on-ramps. That disclosure gap is what holds the {{grade}} overall grade down: the safeguarding structure reads like the top tier's on paper, but the backing pillar grades what is proven, and self-reported reserves with public attestations still 'being prepared' cannot outscore their paperwork, which leaves backing the weakest pillar on the card. Distribution is the counterweight: a deployment sprawling from Ethereum and its L2s to Gnosis, Polygon, Cosmos rails, and Algorand, though DEX depth still tilts toward a couple of dominant pools, a mismatch the peg record documents in a string of brief wobbles. Burning EURe and crediting EUR via SEPA through {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} remains the one exit that never depends on pool depth. The real gap to the top tier is simpler: EURC shows its reserves monthly to a Big Four examiner, and Monerium still asks you to take its word.

eusd-electronic-usd.title: Lending Basket With First-Loss Risk
eusd-electronic-usd.text: eUSD is a Reserve Protocol RToken that combines Compound V3 USDC, Aave V3 USDC, and Compound V3 USDT in equal thirds behind a permissionless basket {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} mechanism, with RSR stakers absorbing first loss: a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} basket whose machinery works better than its report card. The peg record is the strongest line on the card, stress monitoring has historically sat at the calm end of the scale, and atomic permissionless redemption keeps the exit pillar the best of the three; the long tail of historical depeg blips is real but largely ancient, the worst a double-digit gash in earlier days. So why does the {{grade}} overall grade sit where it does? Economic control is the weakest pillar by a wide margin because a 3-of-5 Safe with no timelock holds the central admin role, can grant itself ownership and replace the token implementation instantly, and governs a wrapper that leans entirely on Aave, Compound, and the USDC and USDT underneath. V9 treats that as a first-class risk rather than a footnote. Backing lands in the middle once those dependencies are priced in: pinned on-chain reads confirm the equal-thirds basket to within a hundredth of a point, and the weights remain governance-set and changeable. The design is sound; the pillar that decides the grade is the one key set that can rewrite the rest.

crvusd-curve.title: LLAMMA on Custodial Bitcoin
crvusd-curve.text: crvUSD is Curve's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin with LLAMMA soft-liquidation and deep DEX liquidity, but most collateral is custodial WBTC/cbBTC. When the protocol that dominates stablecoin DEX routing launches its own stablecoin, the design had better be interesting. LLAMMA replaces cliff-edge {{term:liquidation}}liquidations{{/term}} with gradual rebalancing through price bands. The {{grade}} overall grade is solid rather than elite because the collateral story contains a structural contradiction: Bitcoin collateral running through BitGo and Coinbase introduces exactly the centralized {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} dependencies crypto-native collateral was supposed to avoid. PegKeeper pools paired with USDC, USDT, PYUSD, frxUSD, and GHO provide active peg machinery, while scrvUSD creates a yield feedback loop where stress can pull buyers back in. Curve still gives crvUSD one of the deeper on-chain liquidity footprints among CDP dollars, though the exit pillar is the weakest of the three because those routes share a failure domain. Even home-field advantage cannot fully insulate a crypto-backed stablecoin from the deleveraging cycles that govern its borrowers.

gho-aave.title: Aave's Lending-Book Dollar
gho-aave.text: GHO is Aave's decentralized dollar minted by borrowing against Aave collateral: a diversified {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} dollar drawn from the protocol's battle-tested pools. The {{grade}} overall grade splits cleanly across the V9 pillars. Exit is near-flawless because a deeply distributed DEX footprint plus {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}}-style GSM redemption make it about as clean as on-chain exits get, while backing lags at the bottom of the report card, because the collateral is whatever mixed crypto Aave's risk machinery accepts and the largest reserve slice, the mainnet GSM aggregate, does not disclose its underlying stablecoin identities, and economic control prices the governance that steers it all. The long tail of brief sub-peg blips dates from GHO's rocky early months; the peg has long since settled. Development has kept moving: Aave V4 shipped on Ethereum mainnet this spring with its unified-liquidity hub-and-spoke architecture, the sGHO savings vault launched at a fixed rate in April, and a governance proposal would push sGHO cross-chain starting with Arbitrum. Aave proved a lending protocol can birth a credible dollar if it iterates in public; the backing pillar's lag is the bill for letting that dollar lean on the whole lending book.

sources.label: Aave V4 is Live on Ethereum

fdusd-first-digital.title: Binance's Post-BUSD Dollar
fdusd-first-digital.text: FDUSD is a BVI-issued dollar stablecoin backed by short-dated {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}} and cash, custodied by First Digital Trust, and the custodian risk stopped being abstract in April 2025. First Digital USD rose to prominence as Binance's preferred stablecoin after BUSD's regulatory demise, and the lineage worry crystallized when Justin Sun publicly claimed the {{term:custody}}custodian{{/term}} was insolvent: FDUSD broke sharply below par within hours before recovering, and First Digital answered with a Hong Kong defamation suit seeking retractions and damages: a peg defended in court filings as much as in redemption windows. The reserves themselves remain conventional: overwhelmingly short-dated T-bills and cash, {{term:attestation}}attested{{/term}} monthly, most recently by Hong Kong's AOGB for end-June 2026, and backing now grades well on that attested mix. The {{grade}} overall grade shows where Pharos sees the weakness instead: the exit pillar is the weakest of the three, and every reserve account sits with a single related-party custodian, First Digital Trust, while the peg record is among the strongest lines on the card and the depeg history reads as brief episodes rather than chronic drift. Deployed across six chains including Sui, TON, and Solana, the distribution still follows Binance's ecosystem preferences more than organic DeFi demand. FDUSD's fate remains a single-dependency story: Binance's endorsement made it, and one custodian tweet-storm nearly unmade it.

sources.label: CoinDesk: First Digital Trust serves Justin Sun with defamation claim
BeInCrypto: FDUSD depegs to $0.87 after Justin Sun insolvency claims

pyusd-paypal.title: PayPal's Paxos-Issued Dollar
pyusd-paypal.text: PayPal's KPMG-examined PYUSD still carries one of the cleanest reserve profiles Pharos tracks: overnight {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} reverse repos with a cash sleeve underneath, held at Paxos under an OCC national trust charter in segregated, bankruptcy-remote accounts. The exit pillar is the strongest line on the card, with permissionless 1:1 issuer {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}. What holds the {{grade}} overall grade below the reserve quality is the economic-control pillar, the weakest of the three: issuer-direct minting across four native surfaces is economically unbounded and reconciled only against reserves, Paxos administrator paths can change controllers, caps, and token logic, and Pharos records a direct holder-freeze capability. Fourteen further deployments are LayerZero omnichain representations, so the multichain surface adds external validation risk on top of issuer controls. Adoption remains the other open question: the float shrank by roughly a third from its March 2026 peak by early August, which reads more like crypto-native capital rotating out than PayPal's retail network transacting on-chain.

sources.label: Cryptonomist: PYUSD supply near $2.7B in early August 2026, down from $4B+ in March

gyen-gyen.title: Regulated in the Wrong Country
gyen-gyen.text: GYEN is GMO Trust's NYDFS-chartered yen stablecoin backed by FDIC cash and {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}. It has pristine custody, near-zero on-chain usage, and now an orderly wind-down notice. It holds the distinction of being one of the most heavily regulated JPY stablecoins in existence, though the regulator is New York rather than Tokyo. GMO Trust's charter, monthly Network Firm {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}}, and very-low-risk reserve model would be impressive if the market still cared. The problem is the secondary market: thin DEX liquidity and a long depeg history make GYEN trade less like a stablecoin and more like a neglected FX derivative. The 2021 depeg litigation and 2026 wind-down notice turn the dashboard's failing profile into a verdict rather than a warning. This is pristine {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} architecture wrapped around a token whose main remaining use case is redemption before the lights go out.

usdy-ondo-finance.title: Clean Treasuries, Multi-Day Exit
usdy-ondo-finance.text: Ondo's USDY is a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} NAV token for non-U.S. investors, and the spread of its Safety Score pillars explains its record better than the overall line, which currently reads {{grade}}. The backing is about as clean as tokenized {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} exposure gets on paper: Ondo's September 2026 holdings disclosure puts more than 97% in short-term U.S. Treasuries, with a small Ondo Stocks position and a trace of bank deposits, under daily NAV {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} from Ankura Trust. Yet backing is only the middle pillar on the card, because v9 grades the mechanism wrapped around the assets, not just their quality. The exit pillar is the weakest of the three: on-chain liquidity is thin and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} runs through a multi-day, eligibility-gated window at the BVI-domiciled, issuer-controlled structure, despite a footprint spanning more than a dozen networks from Ethereum and Solana to Noble and Mantra. Economic control is the strongest line on the card. There is no hard dollar peg to defend, which is the point of a NAV token that accrues value instead. USDY remains a clean way to hold U.S. government debt for investors American regulators will not let buy it directly; the card prices in that you are trusting Ondo's plumbing, not a market, to get your money back.

sources.label: Ondo USDY holdings and transparency page

cadc-cad-coin.title: Backed by Scanned Bank Letters
cadc-cad-coin.text: CADC has been the on-chain loonie since 2021, with FINTRAC registration as an MSB under the Loon brand, 1:1 redemption against CAD held in trust at ATB Financial, and deployment across six chains including Solana. Its reach is broader than most local-currency stablecoins despite modest circulation. The regulatory waiting game it was built for is over: Canada's Stablecoin Act received royal assent in March 2026 as part of Bill C-15, naming the Bank of Canada as supervisor of stablecoin issuers, though the operative provisions await regulations expected to run into 2027. That timeline cuts both ways for a first mover, because Pharos's data shows the compliance story is thinner than the branding: reserve transparency amounts to monthly scanned bank-confirmation letters with no accountant's opinion and no reconciliation against circulating supply, exit liquidity is close to nonexistent, and the peg has logged a long tail of deviation events: a {{grade}} overall report card despite solid economic-control marks. {{term:redemption}}Redemption{{/term}} 1:1 against trust-held CAD remains the design, and the registry the Bank of Canada will open will decide whether the design is enough. Until the bank letters carry an opinion and a supply reconciliation, the backing evidence stays a confirmation rather than an attestation, and the exit pillar stays the weakest line on the card.

sources.label: DLA Piper: Canada enacts stablecoin framework in Bill C-15 (April 2026)

cadd-cad-digital.title: Canada's Institutional CAD Rail
cadd-cad-digital.text: CADD launched in May 2026 as Canada's first CAD stablecoin issued by a regulated financial institution, Tetra Trust, under Alberta's Loan and Trust Corporations Act, with a backer roster (Shopify, National Bank of Canada, ATB Financial, Wealthsimple) that reads like a who's-who of Canadian fintech. It is now fully live on Pharos rather than coverage-pending, and the data is unusually clean for a long-tail fiat coin: the peg record is the strongest line on the card, and the backing pillar is supported by monthly Baker Tilly reasonable-assurance {{term:attestation}}examinations{{/term}} that reconcile the pooled trust reserve against token liabilities across every chain. The catch is scale and age: circulation remains a rounding error next to that backer roster, the exit pillar is the weakest of the three on the {{grade}} card because an institutional settlement rail has little use for DEX pools until institutions actually settle on it, and a track-record cap applies to a token this young. Issuance is operator-mediated with no on-chain cap or timelock, so the reconciliation rests on the attestation cadence rather than code. With the Stablecoin Act now assented and the Bank of Canada assuming supervision, CADD's bet is that compliant infrastructure built before the rules arrive becomes the default once they do; until then the rail exists and the traffic does not.

sources.label: Business Wire: Tetra Digital Group launches CADD (May 2026)
DLA Piper: Canada enacts stablecoin framework in Bill C-15 (April 2026)

usde-ethena.title: The Basis Trade, Tokenized
usde-ethena.text: Ethena's USDe is still the tokenized {{term:basis-trade}}basis trade{{/term}}, but the current reserve mix is more conservative and more complicated than the original pitch. At the latest live capture, roughly seven eighths of backing sat in a Liquid Cash basket of stablecoins, DeFi lending, tokenized funds, and institutional loans, with the hedged crypto sleeve reduced to a small minority split between ETH and BTC. Ethena publishes the category split but not the weights inside the basket, so most of the reserve is a disclosed mixed basket rather than an itemized one. The hedged sleeve still depends on off-exchange custody at Copper, Ceffu, and Fireblocks and on CEX {{term:perpetual}}perpetual{{/term}} markets. The old contradiction has softened into a {{grade}} overall grade. The exit pillar leads the card, backing sits in the middle, and economic control is the weakest of the three. That pillar is scored on how mint, oracle, and bridge authority are bounded: a one-day timelock owns the token, a 5-of-10 Safe runs it, and the TON deployment gives an administrator the power to lock holder wallets. The peg record is clean, with a handful of brief episodes over a tracking history still short of three years. Ethena's real-time dashboard helps even as custodian attestations run months behind it, but neither turns CEX custody, backend-signed mint flows, or an unitemized basket into neutral facts. USDe's trick is making a risky institutional trade look calm at the token level; the machinery underneath is what the card is scoring.

aeur-anchored-coins.title: Death of a Swiss Euro
aeur-anchored-coins.text: AEUR is Anchored Coins' centralized euro stablecoin, backed by euro reserves at Swissquote Bank SA, but the issuer is in a regulated wind-down with no new issuance. The FlowBank bankruptcy exposure that once complicated the backing has been resolved through that consolidation, yet the operating posture is permanent: MiCAR-era requirements leave a Swiss issuer no obvious reactivation path. Binance, the venue that once gave AEUR its reason to exist, has now completed the unwind, delisting the final spot pair at the end of July 2026 and, from mid-August, switching off withdrawals and auto-converting remaining balances to euros at 1:1. This was less a delisting than an escorted exit. Thin DEX trading and a large minimum for direct issuer {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} make the peg less something a market can repair than a balance sheet the issuer can settle. The reserves may be intact, but when your largest venue converts holders out whether they ask or not, the product is past hospice care. Only an estate sale remains.

sources.label: Binance: Notice Regarding the Removal of AEUR and Conversion of AEUR to EUR

buck-bucket-protocol.title: Sui's Legacy Dollar in Migration
buck-bucket-protocol.text: BUCK is Bucket Protocol's original Sui dollar, minted from {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} vaults against SUI, BTC, ETH, and LSTs, with a {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} swapping USDC and USDT 1:1. It is now a legacy asset: Bucket's current stablecoin is USDB, the official migration converts BUCK to USDB 1:1 with no fee, and the V1 system is in exit-only wind-down with BUCK minting disabled. That conversion path is load-bearing for holders, because the V1 collateral still attributable to BUCK covers only a fraction of outstanding supply and most of it sits in stable-swap LP positions whose BUCK share cannot be separated from the record, so Pharos scores no usable reserve composition. Direct BUCK {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} for collateral keeps the exit pillar the strongest line on the {{grade}} card. Economic control is the weakest: the V1 oracle topology is opaque, with forty registered collateral branches fed by threshold-one Supra or whitelisted-rule oracles, and the admin and upgrade caps sit with team wallets. The peg record is long and scarred, a long tail of episodes including one extreme crash, though recent history has been quiet. The durable question is whether the migration window stays open.

vchf-vnx.title: VNX Franc, Reserve Report Stuck at 2024
vchf-vnx.text: VNX's VCHF is a CHF-redeemable token launched under Liechtenstein's TVTG Blockchain Act, and its evidence trail has stopped moving. The newest reserve report is an AREVA agreed-upon-procedures check as of 31 December 2024, which confirmed aggregate CHF-value coverage in unnamed bank or securities custody accounts without disclosing holdings or category split; the 2025 AREVA cycle covered VNX Gold only, so the fiat series is more than eighteen months stale and outside the v9 freshness bound. Since then VNX suspended exchange operations on 30 June 2026, allowed withdrawals to whitelisted destinations only through July, and moved issuance from VNX Commodities AG to Bermuda-licensed VNX Global Ltd, while circulating VCHF fell to a fraction of the 2024 attested figure. Pharos scores the issuer-controlled mint stack as strong economic control across twelve chains, but backing rests on a stale aggregate and the exit pillar is the weakest of the three: {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} is eligibility-gated, no comparable on-chain route is supported, and pricing confidence is low. The compliance sidecar marks it non-compliant under MiCA as an e-money token. Regulation on paper does not make the reserve legible, and a franc rail whose last reserve check predates its own operational suspension is running on trust.

sources.label: AREVA VNX reserve report as of December 31, 2024

audd-novatti.title: Australia's Compliance Play
audd-novatti.text: AUDD is what happens when an issuer builds a stablecoin the way regulators wish everyone would: AUD cash at Australian deposit-taking institutions, an AFSL from ASIC, and monthly William Buck procedures. The July 2026 report is the anchor Pharos has on file: AUD cash split between a Westpac bare trust held by AMAL Trustees and a Banking Circle account, agreed without exception against on-chain supply across eight networks, with a small excess over liabilities. That evidence carries the {{grade}} overall grade, and the card's shape is unusual for a regional fiat coin: the exit pillar leads, while backing and economic control trail it by a similar margin, the issuer's mint being economically unbounded and reconciled only after the fact. The catch is timing. Pharos admits a composition only while it is fresh, so the card carries a stale-composition ceiling whenever the next monthly report has not yet landed, and the score moves on the calendar rather than on the product. Worth keeping in view: William Buck's engagement is agreed-upon procedures that expressly declines to express an opinion and carries no independence requirement. AUDD's constraint is whether Australia's on-chain economy grows large enough to want a domestic dollar.

sources.label: William Buck: AUDD Agreed-Upon Procedures Report, July 2026

cgusd-cygnus-finance.title: Base's Treasury Wrapper
cgusd-cygnus-finance.text: cgUSD is Cygnus Finance's daily-rebasing T-bill dollar on Base, and the gap between off-chain NAV and on-chain price has produced a long tail of depeg events. The reserve model is described rather than shown: Cygnus states the portfolio holds short-term {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}} off-chain plus on-chain USDC and USDT, but publishes no weights, no custodian name, and no {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, so Pharos carries the whole reserve as one unsplit basket. {{term:redemption}}Redemption{{/term}} at 1:1 in USDC runs through a request-and-claim queue that normally settles in five to seven days after the custodian sells bills. That window is why the rebase cannot erase the arbitrage friction: the on-chain price can drift from NAV while exits wait. The {{grade}} overall grade is held down by the economic-control pillar, the weakest of the three, because the vault and its NAV oracle sit behind a 10-second timelock controlled by a 2-of-11 Safe and the daily NAV that drives supply is issuer-asserted. Institutional-unregulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} with no published proof path leaves the trust assumptions sitting mostly with the Cygnus team. The reserve is an {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} basket; the exit experience is still very much a DeFi product.

fxusd-f-x-protocol.title: Leverage as a Peg Mechanism
fxusd-f-x-protocol.text: fxUSD is f(x) Protocol's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-minted dollar {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} by WBTC and wstETH, with a Stability Pool arbitraging Curve to defend the peg. f(x) Protocol turns leveraged long positions into peg defense: xPOSITION NFTs represent looped exposure to a majority-WBTC collateral mix, while fxUSD holders get the stable side of the trade. The {{grade}} overall grade holds, with backing now the strongest of its three pillars even as WBTC's BitGo/Coinbase custody sits awkwardly inside a nominally decentralized machine. It earns its keep through an atomic {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop and a Stability Pool that actively arbitrages the USDC/fxUSD Curve pool, while dozens of brief depeg blips show the mechanism wobbles but recovers. The exit pillar is the laggard: DEX liquidity remains concentrated enough that one pool failure would gut exit capacity. A clever design that works until vol overwhelms the leverage.

usdb-blast.title: Yield Dollar Stranded on Blast
usdb-blast.text: USDB's reserve is quality stablecoin collateral routed through MakerDAO's DSR, but the product is confined to a single chain. The current metadata models the backing through Blast's DAI yield manager, which is less exotic than the surrounding ecosystem branding would suggest. The depeg history, an unusually long tail of recorded episodes, tells the story of a rebasing stablecoin on an island with no comparable route out. Governance-set yield barely registers against the cost of holding a chain-native wrapper with no issuer-style {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop. Exit is the weakest of the three pillars behind the {{grade}} overall grade, because the deployment is Blast-only and no comparable same-notional route out is supported. The underlying collateral would look respectable in a more liquid wrapper, and the live token contract carries no blacklist or pause function, though its proxy admin can replace the implementation. USDB is a technically competent product on a chain of its own, and the durable constraint is the {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}}: the only way out is back to Ethereum as DAI.

sources.label: Blast documentation (USDB route and DAI bridge redemption)

buidl-blackrock.title: BlackRock's Tokenized Treasury Fund
buidl-blackrock.text: BUIDL is BlackRock's tokenized institutional {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market fund{{/term}}, a Reg D participating share priced at a $1 NAV and backed by U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} bills and overnight tri-party repo with a handful of major bank counterparties, custodied by BNY Mellon and administered by Securitize. Chronicle publishes a daily position-level holdings table, so the reserve is among the most transparent in Pharos and the backing pillar is one of the stronger lines on the {{grade}} card. The card is a reminder that Pharos measures structural risk, not brand prestige. The exit pillar is the weakest of the three: BUIDL is confined to eligible holders, so leaving means a transfer agent, not a market. The binding cap is a dependency finding: the Solana issuance programs share a single immediate EOA upgrade key with other tokenized liabilities Pharos tracks, and the six EVM deployments share one EOA master and upgrader, so issuance is uncapped and controlled by keys rather than contracts. Yield is NAV accretion from the T-bill and repo portfolio, passed through as a rebase. Eight chain deployments via Securitize widen the footprint, with Wormhole carrying issuer-controlled burn-and-reissue transfers rather than wrapped supply. BUIDL's significance is infrastructural: a regulated fund share that other on-chain products can hold as reserve, not an asset most people will ever hold directly.

btcusd-btcfi.title: Bitcoin's CDP Outpost
btcusd-btcfi.text: BtcUSD is BTCfi's {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} USD stablecoin minted from BTC variants through Liquity-style {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} vaults. The backing is all Bitcoin exposure in various wrapped or native forms: native BTC, BTCB, cbBTC, and WBTC, plus a collateral handler the protocol's own registry does not identify, which gives holders hard-money aesthetics plus every {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} assumption those wrappers drag along. Its long tail of depeg episodes makes it one of the noisier CDPs per unit of market relevance. Issued natively on Bifrost, with Base and BSC representations and no modeled {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop, the practical exit route is secondary-market liquidity on chains the broader DeFi market does not heavily visit. Economic control is the weakest pillar on the {{grade}} card: the CDP handler's owner can swap its logic target immediately with no timelock, the documentation publishes no shutdown or bad-debt procedure, and the Base token carries owner-set blacklist and pause switches. The question remains whether BTC holders will trust yet another wrapping layer when established CDPs already accept wrapped Bitcoin with better liquidity and peg infrastructure.

usbd-bima.title: BTC Collateral, CDP Ambitions
usbd-bima.text: USBD is a Liquity-style {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin minted from overcollateralized vaults of Bitcoin wrappers, with permissionless {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} against the lowest-ratio vaults and a {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} for near-1:1 stablecoin swaps. At the last fixed capture the entire collateral book sat in the WBTC wrapper branch, so the live {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} assumption is WBTC's custodians, while the liquid-staking and restaking collateral in the marketing held no balance. Backing is nevertheless the strongest of the three pillars, priced through Chainlink BTC/USD under a 150% minimum ratio. What drags the {{grade}} overall grade down is economic control, the weakest pillar on the card: the BimaCore owner is a single EOA that can mint USBD directly without limit, install new mint adapters, and raise debt ceilings, and the DebtToken lets protocol-authorized paths burn an arbitrary holder balance. Exit sits in the middle, with a structurally sound redemption backstop but a secondary market too thin to test it. The peg has held at par so far, which says as much about trading volume as about the mechanism. The durable constraint is the owner key: Liquity mechanics assume nobody can mint around them, and here someone can.

sources.label: Bima mainnet addresses and collateral registry

doc-money-on-chain.title: Bitcoin, Not Bank Deposits
doc-money-on-chain.text: DOC is Money On Chain's rBTC-collateralized dollar on Rootstock and one of the cleaner hard-money stablecoin designs in the tracked set: no bank reserve story, no fiat {{term:custody}}custodian{{/term}}, just rBTC locked inside Money On Chain and a protocol that lets holders move back into Bitcoin-sidechain collateral when they want out. That simplicity cuts both ways. DOC's reserve logic is easier to trust than most small fiat tokens, but its market depth, chain reach, and surrounding infrastructure are far thinner than mainstream dollar stablecoins, and the {{grade}} overall grade carries a reminder from April 2026, when a consensus-bypass flaw in the OMoC price oracle forced a protocol panic pause before the fix. DOC is small, and it matters less as a payments network than as proof that Bitcoin-collateralized dollars are still alive outside Ethereum's orbit. Mechanically DOC is a {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} against rBTC with {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} and permissionless {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} for rBTC; economic control is the weakest of the three pillars because governance can upgrade mint-critical logic through the Money On Chain Governor.

usdrif-rif.title: The RIF-Collateralized Dollar
usdrif-rif.text: USDRIF is a Rootstock {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin minted against RIF token collateral, which pushes the Rootstock stablecoin experiment further out on the risk curve than DOC: RIF rather than Bitcoin stands behind the peg, so everything stays onchain and transparent while the reserve is much weaker in quality. The protocol docs support minting and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} through {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} positions exposed to {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} risk, and the on-chain collateral bucket is readable at any block, which is why the exit pillar leads the {{grade}} card while the volatile single-asset reserve keeps backing behind it. The structure is still niche: small, volatile-collateral-backed, and dependent on a market that has never reached real scale. That makes USDRIF worth tracking as a live Rootstock stablecoin rather than a safe haven.

isc-international-stable-currency.title: The Anti-Dollar Experiment
isc-international-stable-currency.text: ISC deliberately rejects the dollar peg and tries to stabilize purchasing power through a basket of gold, investment-grade bonds, short-term T-bills, global equities, and cash, so its nominal price is designed to drift upward over time. Pharos treats it as a NAV-style {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} token rather than a par dollar. What the issuer dashboard shows is less reassuring than the philosophy. As fetched in August 2026, close to half of the combined reserve holdings were ISC tokens held by the reserve itself, which Pharos treats as circular self-reserve rather than external backing, with the remainder spread across iShares and Vanguard ETFs and USD cash at undisclosed custodians. The dashboard is undated, mutable, and unaudited, and the issuer says an audit scheme is still under consideration. Backing and exit are the two weak pillars on the {{grade}} report card, the first on that reserve evidence and the second on the absence of a comparable same-notional route, while economic control fares better because the Solana mint sits behind an immutable 2-of-3 SPL multisig with no upgradeable program in the path. The catch remains a retained freeze authority, Solana-only issuance, institutional-unregulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, and no published holder loss waterfall or recovery process. The durable constraint is that a purchasing-power target is only as good as the reserve that is supposed to buy it.

usd0-usual.title: USYC Behind the Wrappers
usd0-usual.text: USD0 is Usual's {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}}-backed dollar. The approved collateral list spans Hashnote USYC, M0's M, and Ethena's USDtb, the latter two held through Usual's own wrapper contracts, with USDC as the deposit gateway, but the last fixed on-chain capture resolved the entire book to USYC, a tokenised share of a {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}}-bill and reverse-repo fund custodied at BNY Mellon through Marex. Every supposedly boring component arrives with another issuer's operating model attached, and that is what the card prices in: backing is the weakest of the three pillars because the claim runs into an upstream fund share whose own score caps what USD0 can inherit. Economic control sits mid-card, with 8-of-15 Safes over role grants and the upgrade path and an unbounded DaoCollateral mint role. The genuine structural strength is exit: the permissionless {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path through DaoCollateral leads the card, so holders can leave at will even when secondary markets wobble, as a long tail of recorded episodes shows they periodically do. France-domiciled and architecturally ambitious, USD0 carries a {{grade}} overall grade that reflects several low-risk parts failing to add up to one cleaner whole. The durable constraint is that USD0 can never be safer than the fund it wraps.

usr-resolv.title: Frozen at Sixteen Cents
usr-resolv.text: Resolv's USR was a {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}} synthetic dollar with an RLP insurance layer; it collapsed in 2026 after an EOA-minter exploit produced 80M unbacked tokens and depegged the asset, and the token was frozen. Resolv's USR was a {{term:basis-trade}}basis trade{{/term}}-driven synthetic dollar whose RLP insurance layer was supposed to absorb negative {{term:funding-rate}}funding rate{{/term}} pressure and protect USR holders until an EOA-minter exploit produced 80M unbacked tokens and shattered the peg. By the time of the freeze, USR had collapsed to $0.164, an 83.6% deviation from its dollar target. The permanent record shows 25 depeg events, including a worst of 9,025 basis points. Supply was volatile in the months leading up to the failure, swinging from $17.5M to $28.4M to $22.3M, the kind of oscillation that suggested frantic positioning rather than organic growth. The irony was sharp: Apostro real-time reserve verification and permissionless atomic {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} with an 82-rated backstop were still technically intact on a token trading at sixteen cents before being frozen. The {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} of the {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}} margin via off-exchange settlement partners did not save the synthetic when the EOA minter was compromised. Six-chain deployment across Ethereum, Base, BSC, Berachain, HyperEVM, and Arbitrum meant the failure was visible everywhere, not just somewhere.

usdz-anzen.title: Private Credit Meets DeFi
usdz-anzen.text: Anzen's USDz is backed 1:1 by SPCT, a permissioned token representing a portfolio of U.S. private-credit ABS: SMB merchant receivables, factored invoices, auto leases, consumer installment lending, and litigation finance. Pharos's July 2026 on-chain read found SPCT supply covering USDz supply at roughly 101%, with no {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} or cash sleeve beside it, and the issuer publishes no SPCT valuation methodology or mark cadence. A mediocre peg grade and hundreds of recorded depeg events make USDz one of the more frequently depegged stablecoins on the dashboard. Qualified Market Makers mint at 1:1 USDz/USDC while retail relies on DEX arbitrage to close the gap. It is a two-tier system that works when the market trusts the collateral and breaks when it doesn't. The yield from private credit is real and uncorrelated with crypto markets, but so is the liquidity mismatch between 90-day {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} receivables and instant {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} expectations against self-reported transparency alone.

ausd-agora.title: VanEck's Quiet Dollar
ausd-agora.text: AUSD is Agora's centralized dollar stablecoin, redeemable 1:1 and backed by cash, short-dated U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasury bills{{/term}}, and overnight repos managed by VanEck. The institutional stack is unusually explicit: VanEck manages the reserves, State Street provides {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} through a bankruptcy-remote Delaware Statutory Trust, and Grant Thornton publishes monthly {{term:attestation}}reserve attestations{{/term}} rather than a token-specific real-time proof feed. Holders still rely on an issuer, an asset manager, a custodian, and a periodic accountant across a multichain footprint. That is a cleaner chain than many fiat-backed dollars offer, but it is still a chain. AUSD holds a {{grade}} overall grade, with the exit pillar leading the card and backing the weakest of the three: the May 2026 report puts most of the reserve in Treasury repurchase agreements with undisclosed counterparties, plus a small stablecoin slice whose issuers are not named. The peg record is long and quiet, with a tail of brief episodes clustered in its first year. AUSD's transparency runs on monthly attestations rather than a live on-chain reserve window.

sources.label: Grant Thornton Agora Dollar Reserve Report - May 31, 2026

usds-sky.title: The PSM Moat Deepens
usds-sky.text: Sky Dollar still commands the single best {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} infrastructure in stablecoins: a permissionless {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} with atomic, zero-fee settlement and well over half of total supply available as immediate exit capacity. No other stablecoin at scale offers anything close. The {{grade}} safety grade reflects strength tempered by where the cracks actually are, with a reserve mix split across PSM stablecoins, Spark lending {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} positions, and Grove {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} allocations providing genuine diversification rather than the concentration risk that plagues most competitors. The peg itself is the easy part. USDS has stayed at the calm end of the stress scale and clears its worst sub-day wobbles within hours, with a long tail of brief deviations whose most recent entry is well over a year old. The yield-to-risk story through the Sky Savings Rate still rewards holders without the exotic risk profiles that higher-yielding alternatives require. The structural dependency on USDC as mechanism-critical PSM collateral remains the one tension in a DAO-governed system that aspires to monetary sovereignty. Roughly two-fifths of Sky Dollar's backing sits in the PSM stablecoin bucket, with Sky Agent allocations to Grove credit and Spark lending making up most of the rest.

m-m0.title: The Middleware Dollar
m-m0.text: M0's M is an institutional dollar stablecoin minted 1:1 by permissioned Minters against eligible collateral, principally short-term U.S. {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}} and cash held in bankruptcy-remote SPVs, with on-chain Validator attestations replacing periodic audits. The peg record is the strongest line on the card, and the exit pillar leads the three because issuer redeemability gives holders a route that spot depth alone would not suggest; direct M liquidity stays institution-facing rather than pooled on DEXes, so Pharos leaves it unrated on liquidity. Backing is now the weakest pillar, and the reason is disclosure rather than asset quality: M0's current Protocol API publishes the aggregate collateral total but no longer exposes the cash-versus-Treasury split or minter-level provider shares. The reviewed structure also routes more than 90% of collateral through one Superstate and UMB Bank chain, which Pharos classifies as institutional-unregulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. Permissioned Minters lock collateral while Validators cryptographically attest sufficiency on-chain, a trust architecture that swaps auditor snapshots for protocol-level verification: elegant, but it concentrates control in a permissioned issuer set, and the Solana representation is frozen by default with thawing limited to approved earners. The {{grade}} overall grade reflects that mix. M's significance is downstream: it anchors the M0 infrastructure cohort of branded and wrapped dollars built on the same {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} rail.

usdm-moneta.title: Peg in Name Only
usdm-moneta.text: Moneta's USDM is the dashboard's cleanest example of pristine reserves failing to create a usable peg. The backing is regulator-friendly: roughly 80% {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market funds{{/term}} run by Fidelity, Western Asset Management, and Amundi, 20% USD bank deposits, an e-money licence in Norway with MiCA EMT authorization still pending, and a Charli3 oracle {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} before each Cardano mint. The problem is brutally simple: with no meaningful observable DEX liquidity, there are no arbitrageurs to enforce the peg, so the price wanders wherever thin order books take it. The {{grade}} overall grade follows the exit pillar, the weakest of the three, with a peg record graded at the bottom of the scale beside it; even backing is held down by disclosure rather than asset quality, because the issuer names no active custodian. Multi-day issuer settlement compounds the exit risk for anyone holding meaningful size. USDM is a well-backed IOU trading at whatever the market feels like, which is a stablecoin only in the most technical and least comforting sense.

satusd-river.title: Omni-CDP Without Stablecoin Collateral
satusd-river.text: River's satUSD is an Omni-{{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin that refuses centralized stablecoin collateral and accepts BTC, ETH, BNB, and liquid staking tokens only. The architecture lets users deposit collateral on one chain and mint satUSD on another through LayerZero {{term:bridge}}bridging{{/term}}, which expands distribution across eleven deployments while importing the usual cross-chain assumptions. The {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop offers permissionless access to blue-chip collateral through {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} positions, and the exit pillar leads the card as a result. The peg record shows a long tail of secondary-market wobbles, and minimal DEX liquidity across many chains leaves the secondary market thin. The weakest pillar is economic control: a single River owner key holds upgrade powers across the native deployments, and collateral pricing runs through single-source oracle paths with no automatic failover. Backing is capped as well, because River publishes no dated split of the collateral basket. That is why the {{grade}} overall grade sits below what the collateral rules alone would suggest. The durable constraint is that principled collateral does not substitute for disclosed composition or bounded control.

usdf-astherus.title: One Exchange, One Exit
usdf-astherus.text: Aster's USDF, issued under the Astherus name before the rebrand, is a Binance-routed {{term:basis-trade}}basis-trade{{/term}} stablecoin: USDT deposited at mint sits in Ceffu {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, is mirrored to a Binance sub-account through MirrorX, and is deployed into long-spot-plus-short-{{term:perpetual}}perpetual{{/term}} positions on that one exchange. Collateral, hedge, and the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop all run through a single pipeline. The peg is the easy part: the peg record is the strongest line on the card, with only a handful of brief, modest deviations over the tracking window. The danger is structural, and the report card says so with a {{grade}} overall grade. The binding constraint is the oracle: Aster publishes no price-feed topology for the system-wide valuation and rebalancing that keeps the reserve {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}}, and Pharos caps the grade at the failing line until it does. Beneath that cap, backing is weak because Aster names its custodian and venue but publishes no itemized balances, provider shares, or independent custody reconciliation, and no attestation gives current weights for retained USDT, spot crypto, or futures margin. Economic control is weak on the same unpublished oracle and a token whose administrator can pause every transfer. The exit pillar is the least bad of the three, but a BSC-only deployment with a dormant bridge rail leaves holders dependent on the issuer's USDT redemption the moment the Binance-Ceffu pipeline hiccups. USDF is a yield product with a stablecoin's ticker, and everything that matters about it happens off-chain on one exchange.

usda-avalon.title: The BTC-Backed Misnomer
usda-avalon.text: Avalon USDa calls itself a BTC-backed CDP, but the reserve mix is messier: FBTC custody exposure, a large USDT leg, and assorted BTC LSTs all sit under the Bitcoin banner. The design adds 1:1 USDT convertibility, Redstone-priced collateral, HFT liquidation machinery, and LayerZero bridge distribution, which is a lot of plumbing for a token marketed as simple Bitcoin-backed dollars. Pharos keeps the collateral-quality view conservative because wrapped BTC, centralized stablecoin exposure, and permissioned mint controls are not the same thing as holding native BTC in a trustless vault. The interesting contradiction is that the liquidation machinery can look sophisticated while the holder still depends on Cobo, Fireblocks, Coinbase Prime, role-gated minting, and cross-chain infrastructure behaving well at the same time. Lately the room has been emptying: price coverage has thinned to the point where Pharos treats the peg deviation as unobservable rather than at par, and with the exit and economic-control pillars both at the bottom of the scale, the collateral book is the only pillar still above water. The {{grade}} overall grade follows from that. Nobody published an incident report; the exits are simply visible on-chain, with DefiLlama's adapter measuring a few dollars of on-chain reserves against the reported circulating supply. It is a Bitcoin stablecoin in the way a finance committee is a wallet: technically connected to the asset, heavily mediated by everyone in the room.

sources.label: Avalon USDa risk management (custodians, LTV parameters)

usdtb-ethena.title: The Load-Bearing Wall
usdtb-ethena.text: USDtb is the stable ballast in Ethena's reserve structure, designed chiefly to be held by its parent protocol rather than traded as a retail DeFi dollar. Its reserve is almost entirely BlackRock's BUIDL, with a small cash settlement float, issued by Anchorage Digital Bank with BUIDL self-custodied in segregated wallets and cash in segregated fiduciary accounts at undisclosed banks. That puts short-dated U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasuries{{/term}} behind the token, but through a deliberately long chain of funds, custodians, issuer controls, and Ethena risk management. Direct mint-and-redeem rails and BUIDL's atomic redemption are useful exits, though they do not turn the product into a broadly liquid consumer asset, which is why exit is the weakest of the three pillars on the {{grade}} card.
