The old editorial worry, that a micro-cap CDP is too small to attract the arbitrage that turns redemption into a real peg floor, turned out to be the entire story: fixed-rate credit at that scale could not generate enough borrowing to sustain the machine around it. Credit where due, collateral redemption stayed open throughout, making this that rarest of DeFi endings: solvent, orderly, and announced in advance.

usdaf-asymmetry.title: Immutable CDP, Recursive Collateral
usdaf-asymmetry.text: USDaf is an immutable Liquity V2 {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} minted from yield-bearing stablecoin and BTC collateral, structurally pure but still market-small. The collateral stack is recursive by design: ysyBOLD dominates, scrvUSD is material, sUSDS adds Sky exposure, and smaller tBTC, sfrxUSD, and WBTC slices round out the book. The contracts are immutable with ownership renounced, no admin can freeze a balance or register a new minter, and the branches carry conservative {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}}, so backing and exit both score well. What binds the {{grade}} overall grade is size: circulating supply has sat below Pharos's $1M floor, so peg deviation is withheld by design and the rating is capped until the market grows past it. The price of recursive decentralization remains steep: limited circulation, recurring depeg blips, and a market that does not always route sellers cleanly to the Liquity V2 {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} floor. The permissionless collateral-redemption backstop is structurally sound and {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} mechanics inherit Liquity's design. USDaf is one of the purest expressions of trustless stablecoin design currently live; the recurring depeg blips price what that purity costs in market depth.

usnd-nerite.title: Immutable Code, Invisible Scale
usnd-nerite.text: Nerite's USND was a Liquity-V2 fork {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} dollar on Arbitrum, built on immutable contracts with permissionless collateral {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} and, for a while, one of the cleanest decentralization-and-dependency profiles a nine-figure stablecoin could ask for. That profile is now academic: USND is frozen and carries an F across the board, the grade an archived asset earns once there is nothing left to score. The cause was structural rather than monetary. One approved collateral branch leaned on rsETH, and when the rsETH hack impaired it, immutable code meant Nerite could not patch the market away or rewrite the risk controls. Supply collapsed from a ~$2.7M peak to under $100K, and with such a thin exit door, the {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-style {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} and {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} machinery had no scale left to defend the peg. DEWS still sits at the calm end of the stress scale, but that reading reflects the frozen, inactive market rather than a healthy peg. USND was the answer to a question very few people were asking: whether you can build a truly decentralized, immutable stablecoin that scores well on every metric except the one that requires other people to care. The rsETH hack settled it: contracts nobody could amend had no way to shed the impaired branch, and what remains is under $100K of frozen supply.

ftusd-flying-tulip.title: On-Chain Carry, Concentrated Control
ftusd-flying-tulip.text: ftUSD is Flying Tulip's non-yielding base dollar, while sftUSD is the optional wrapper that receives strategy yield. The live reserve stack lends stablecoin collateral and runs borrow-and-stake carry on both Ethereum and Sonic: WETH into wstETH exposure on Ethereum and wS into stS on Sonic, not a short-perpetual hedge. Flying Tulip's token-sale capital is not conventional operating runway: primary FT allocations carry a perpetual put against reserved contributed assets, and the issuer says operations are funded from generated yield and revenue. Yield attributable to unstaked ftUSD accrues to the protocol, an opportunity-cost transfer distinct from a mandatory yield-bearing token. Flying Tulip indexes the reserve feed, while the underlying balances are publicly verifiable on-chain. The remaining risks include lending and staking/liquidation exposure, upstream USDC/USDT/USSD dependencies, and the same no-timelock 3-of-5 Safe controlling token ownership, master-minter authority, and the upgradeable minter on both chains.

brla-brla-digital.title: Avenia's Audited Real
brla-brla-digital.text: BRLA is Avenia's centralized Brazilian real stablecoin, minted and redeemed 1:1 for BRL after KYC and deployed natively on Polygon, Gnosis, Celo, and Moonbeam without wrapping or bridge dependencies. Most stablecoins help users leave a local currency for dollars; BRLA tokenizes the real for on-chain settlement instead. The reserve disclosure is stronger than most emerging-market fiat coins: UHY Bendoraytes issues monthly reasonable-assurance reports that itemize BRL cash across named Brazilian banks and payment institutions plus overnight repurchase agreements collateralized by corporate debentures, and reconcile the total against BRLA in circulation. That supports a backing pillar in the upper half of the card. The weak line is exit: on the {{grade}} card the exit pillar is the weakest of the three because no comparable secondary route is established for the supply, so the practical way out is Avenia's own redemption window. Issuance is issuer-direct on every chain, gated by an operator role held by Avenia keys and contracts, with blacklist and upgrade authority in the same hands. The native BRL peg record shows a handful of episodes since Pharos began native-quote monitoring in mid-2026. The trust model remains considerably more traditional than the rails.

silk-shade-protocol.title: The Vault Nobody Can Liquidate
silk-shade-protocol.text: SILK is still the most conceptually ambitious basket stablecoin on Pharos: a GDP-weighted basket of major currencies, gold, and bitcoin, defended by {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} vaults, running natively on Secret Network's privacy chain. It is also, on inspection, a nineteen-vault lending book priced through a single oracle provider with no failover and an empty deviation-guard list. The finding that matters sits in the WBTC vault, second-largest at 18.3% of ShadeLend's elastic debt: it is governance-frozen against roughly 37.9k SILK of debt backed by about 0.00002 WBTC, its {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} query reverts on a divide-by-zero, and its collateral staleness tolerance has been widened from the 600 seconds every other vault uses to a number with fourteen digits. The check is off. Two more collateral oracles have been rejecting queries as stale since February 2025 and July 2026 respectively, and the Stability Pool holds well under half the protocol's aggregate debt with no documented socialization path for a shortfall. Since 18 August 2026 Pharos has also held SILK out of the active set: the upstream CoinGecko and DefiLlama circulating-supply feed has been invalid, roughly twelve times understated, since 5 August, and the listing stays withheld until that source recovers. A multi-currency basket is an elegant answer to a question nobody was asking; a stranded vault with the staleness check disabled is a plainer problem.

idrx-idrx.title: Rupiah Rails With Accountant Reports
idrx-idrx.text: IDRX is PT IDRX Indo Inovasi's rupiah stablecoin, backed 1:1 by IDR held across Indonesian bank deposits, balances at local exchanges and payment firms, and an Indonesian government bond, with KYC-gated mint and redemption through the issuer. The reserve disclosure is more specific than most local-currency coins offer: a July 2026 agreed-upon-procedures report from a registered public accountant itemised seven reserve rows totalling just over 101% of circulating supply, though it is explicitly not an audit opinion and does not establish segregation or bankruptcy remoteness. Backing is nonetheless the weakest pillar on the {{grade}} report card, held back by the age of the independently reviewed composition rather than by what it contains. Exit leads the card, with a permissionless route out. The control surface is centralized: minting is issuer-controlled through per-chain Safes, an ops key holds the admin role that can regrant minter and upgrader rights without delay, and the issuer runs its own burn-and-mint bridge across eight chains with no third-party validator. The peg record is close to spotless. IDRX is credible local payment infrastructure, and the durable constraint is that every reconciliation runs through the issuer.

sources.label: IDRX Reserve Transparency Report July 2026 (agreed-upon procedures)

mxnb-juno.title: Peso Stablecoin, New Issuer Jurisdiction
mxnb-juno.text: MXNB is a 1:1 Mexican peso stablecoin with quarterly reserve {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}} and a multichain FiatToken-style deployment across Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum, Avalanche, and Base. The material change is issuer jurisdiction: beginning April 8, 2026, MXNB says issuance moved to Nvio Pagos El Salvador, S.A. de C.V., an authorised digital-asset issuer in El Salvador. The reserves are still described as Mexican peso assets held with regulated financial institutions under bank {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, so Pharos keeps the fiat-backed model while updating the regulatory owner from Mexico/CNBV to El Salvador/CNAD. The {{grade}} overall grade rests on a strong economic-control pillar and a clean peg record; backing is the weakest of the three pillars because the quarterly BDO Mexico report is a valuation engagement that expressly does not confirm balances with banks and names Nvio and Hey Banco without splitting the balance between them. Mint, master-minter, and proxy-admin rights on Ethereum and Arbitrum sit with issuer-controlled EOAs rather than a multisig. The durable constraint is that an authorised issuer label does not substitute for bank-confirmed reserves.

cjpy-yamato.title: ETH-Backed Yen, Quietly Running
cjpy-yamato.text: CJPY is Yamato's decentralized JPY stablecoin from ETH-only {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}s, built by DeFiGeek Community Japan without a corporate issuer. The mechanism echoes Liquity's playbook: deposit ETH at 130% minimum collateralization, borrow CJPY with a one-time fee and no accruing interest, and use accumulated protocol fees to absorb underwater positions. Its {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} route lets CJPY return one yen worth of ETH from the riskiest pledge, giving the peg an on-chain floor without a bank account. The {{grade}} overall grade is set by the economic-control pillar, the weakest of the three: upgrade authority over Yamato and CurrencyOS sits with a 2-of-4 Safe, and the already-bound CurrencyOS route can burn any holder's CJPY balance without allowance, so the design has no named blacklist but does have an operator with reach. Ethereum-only deployment and a niche circulation keep it philosophically closer to RAI and LUSD than to the centralized yen issuers dominating the category. The mechanism is clean; the open question is whether a clean design remains a specialist instrument rather than a liquid currency.

usdkg-gold-dollar.title: Kyrgyz Gold, Dollar Wrapper
usdkg-gold-dollar.text: USDKG is a Kyrgyz Republic gold-backed stablecoin and a sovereign experiment in commodity-backed design. The Ministry of Finance sold 376 kilograms of LBMA Good Delivery gold bars to LLC Virelint Group, which stores them in sealed boxes at an unnamed bank, and the state-owned OJSC "Issuer of Virtual Assets" mints USD-pegged tokens against that pile. The gold is real. Kyrgyzaltyn, the state mining monopoly that refined it, has been LBMA-listed since 2022. The trust chain from bullion to token runs through private intermediaries whose bank won't even let auditors see the access logs. Kreston Digital Assets' report is an ISRS 4400 agreed-upon procedures engagement, not an audit {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, and it explicitly disclaims assurance. That distinction matters when 100.6% overcollateralization is the only buffer between a gold price dip and undercollateralization. The ConsenSys Diligence smart contract audit found no critical issues but confirmed what the architecture implies: owner multisig can pause all transfers, compliance multisig can blacklist any address and destroy its tokens. At {{supplyUsd}} across Tron and Ethereum with thin DEX-only liquidity, USDKG is less a stablecoin for DeFi and more a cross-border payments rail for Central Asian corridors. Confidence in Bishkek's gold vaults must match the confidence inspired by Brink's London.

usdh-hermetica.title: A Stacks Dollar Backed by Tokenized Credit
usdh-hermetica.text: Hermetica's USDh is a synthetic dollar on Stacks whose documentation still describes a BTC {{term:basis-trade}}basis trade{{/term}}: spot BTC hedged with short {{term:perpetual}}perpetual{{/term}} futures, with {{term:funding-rate}}funding{{/term}} flowing to sUSDh stakers. The disclosed holdings say something else. Hermetica's August 2026 custodian attestation reports the Copper and Ceffu accounts at zero and about ninety-four percent of backing in STRCx, a tokenized digital-credit instrument with exposure to Strategy, Inc., issued by Backed Assets through Kraken's xStocks. The rest is a small USDC reserve fund and an unitemized remainder. A dollar token concentrated in one tokenized security is a different risk than a hedged BTC book. The {{grade}} overall grade is pinned at the failing line by a binding oracle cap: the protocol-wide risk engine that values assets and can pause redemptions publishes no price-feed topology. Beneath the cap, the exit pillar is the weakest of the three, with KYC-gated minting and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} through Hermetica's app, one chain, and no comparable exit route, while backing carries limited evidence because the attestation reconciles only partially to liabilities. The peg has not wavered over the tracking window, on a single price source. The durable constraint is that USDh is whatever its operator decides to hold, and the attestation is the only way to find out.

usdsc-startale.title: Sony's Dollar, M0's Plumbing
usdsc-startale.text: USDSC is a Soneium-exclusive 1:1 wrapper around M0's M, carrying the same short-term {{term:treasury}}Treasury-bill backing{{/term}}, Validator {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}}, and bankruptcy-remote SPV structure into Startale's app ecosystem. It is less a fresh reserve design than a distribution wager: give Sony's L2 a branded dollar, add freeze authority and local integrations, and hope chain gravity supplies the demand. The wrapper inherits M0's backing quality while adding Startale's operator and single-chain dependencies, a reminder that institutional plumbing can still acquire a new control surface at every layer. Whether Soneium needs its own M0 wrapper is unresolved; on the Pharos card the wrapper cannot rate above M itself, so the lineage sets the ceiling and every added layer can only subtract from it.

ctusd-citrea.title: Bitcoin's Dollar, MoonPay's Rails
ctusd-citrea.text: ctUSD is Citrea's native dollar issued by MoonPay on M0, backed by T-bill assets with a broad fiat on-ramp, but still small on a young Bitcoin ZK-rollup. The infrastructure is standard M0: bankruptcy-remote SPVs, on-chain Validator {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}}, short-term {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} backing, the same infrastructure that now underwrites a growing family of branded dollars across the ecosystem. Circulation remains small on a single chain, so the value proposition is still distribution over destination: MoonPay's 30 million-plus verified users can buy in via Visa, Mastercard, Apple Pay, Google Pay, and PayPal across 49 U.S. states and 160-plus countries, an on-ramp far wider than the destination chain's current user base. Founders Fund and Galaxy sit on Citrea's cap table, lending the institutional credibility that typically accompanies products ten times this size. The report card catches the real tension: a spotless peg and solid economic control are pulled down to a {{grade}} overall grade by middling backing evidence and an exit pillar that is the weakest of the three. Reserves are an {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} short-Treasury claim through M0, but {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} runs back through MoonPay's fiat rails or a DEX market that barely exists, and Pharos has no comparable same-notional route to score.

sources.label: Citrea: Introducing ctUSD (MoonPay user base, payment rails, coverage, backers)

usdat-saturn.title: Saylor's Yield, PYUSD Underneath
usdat-saturn.text: Saturn's USDat is a permissioned dollar token whose reserve changed in August 2026. It launched as an M0 extension holding tokenised {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}} in a bankruptcy-remote SPV; at Ethereum block 25789911 Saturn upgraded the proxy to a MultiMint implementation and wound the M reserve down to zero, so the proxy now holds PYUSDx, the MoonPay-issued M0 token backed by PayPal USD, and fixed-block reads reconcile it exactly to USDat supply. The base token is therefore a serial claim on PYUSD, and the {{grade}} overall grade is bound by that parent, since a child cannot rate above the asset it wraps. Backing is the weakest of the three pillars because Saturn publishes a self-reported reserve dashboard rather than an independent reconciliation. The actual Saylor exposure sits one floor up in the sUSDat vault, which rotates capital into STRC, Strategy's perpetual preferred equity, through Clear Street {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and a Securitize-administered BVI fund. Bitcoin's June slide pushed Strategy to a discount to its own bitcoin stack, STRC traded well below par in July, and a vault reported to be concentrated in the preferred was marked around ninety cents on the dollar, while base USDat held at par throughout. USDat stays permissioned, with KYC-gated mint and redemption and compliance whitelist, freeze, and forced-transfer controls retained in the upgraded contract. The durable constraint is that base USDat is only as good as PYUSD, and the yield above it is only as good as Saylor's preferred.

sources.label: Forbes: DeFi stablecoin operation built on Saylor's preferred stock on shaky ground (2026-07-28)
Saturn Dollar current implementation and PYUSDx migration runbook
M0 and MoonPay PYUSDx backing announcement

usdk-orki.title: Stranded on a Dead Chain
usdk-orki.text: Orki's USDK brought Liquity V2-style CDP mechanics to Swellchain, minted against WETH, weETH, rswETH, and swETH. Branch assignments are immutable, the protocol has no individual admin mint path, and collateral redemption is permissionless. This is the full Liquity ethos in miniature. The purity turned out to be the trap: Swellchain closed its bridge-withdrawal window on June 23, 2026 and ended chain operations on June 30, and an immutable protocol had no way to follow its users anywhere else. USDK never had a verified deployment outside Swellchain, so Pharos now carries it as a frozen, abandoned single-chain CDP. Any remaining positions depend on direct contract access against a network that has wound down. The design was honest minimalist plumbing whose single point of failure was the host chain itself, the one variable no amount of governance minimalism could control. Immutability meant the warning label was permanent; now so is the tombstone.

usdq-quill.title: Scroll's Liquity Outpost
usdq-quill.text: Quill's USDQ deploys Liquity V2's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} blueprint on Scroll, minting against wETH, wstETH, weETH, and notably SCR, the host chain's own token. In practice the collateral book is almost entirely wstETH, so LST collateral is the real exposure; accepting SCR at all, however small its current share, ties the stablecoin's health to sentiment around the very network hosting it, a reflexivity loop that gets uncomfortable in a drawdown. Liquity-style dynamic {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} fees preserve the permissionless mechanics, while branch governance and Scroll's own maturity remain part of the control and infrastructure story. The {{grade}} overall grade follows the economic-control pillar, the weakest of the three, with exit close behind: a mutable, multisig-gated upgrade path and a high centralized-mint signal hold the card well below what the collateral alone would earn. The thesis is that Scroll needs a native {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} dollar and a known architecture is the most familiar starting point. The harder question is whether the market needs another Liquity outpost badly enough to build durable exit liquidity around it.

chfau-allunity.title: BaFin-Licensed Franc, Unaudited Reserves
chfau-allunity.text: CHFAU extends the Deutsche Boerse consortium's stablecoin ambitions from the euro to the Swiss franc: the same DWS-Galaxy-Flow Traders alliance behind EURAU, regulated under the same BaFin EMI license, with CHF reserves held 1:1 in segregated accounts at CRR credit institutions and statutory par {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} under MiCA Article 49. MiCA's EMT rules prohibit interest on holdings, so CHFAU competes on trust infrastructure rather than {{term:yield-bearing}}yield{{/term}}, and distribution has moved fast: launched on Ethereum in February 2026, live on Base since July via Coinbase's apps alongside Polygon, Tempo, and Solana deployments. The gap is evidentiary: AllUnity's trust center still lists the independent reserve audit as coming soon, and without a dated report or a published cash-versus-HQLA split, Pharos's backing pillar grades the paperwork rather than the license, which is why backing is the weakest of the three pillars. The {{grade}} overall grade lands on an issuer whose entire pitch is institutional-grade infrastructure. The peg record is spotless so far, but the bank identities, allocations, and successor-custody mechanics remain unpublished, and until a dated reserve report appears the franc is only as verifiable as the promise behind it.

sources.label: AllUnity: CHFAU goes live on Base (July 2026)

buck-buck-assets.title: The Bitcoin Dollar Bet
buck-buck-assets.text: BUCK was Bridge Building's USDC-redeemable savings stablecoin backed by Strategy Inc. preferred stock (STRC) before its April 2026 wind-down. BUCK billed itself as "the world's first SavingsCoin": a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} stablecoin whose treasury was 77% Strategy Inc. perpetual preferred stock, making it less a dollar and more a leveraged view on MicroStrategy's Bitcoin conviction with a dollar wrapper. The yield story (targeting 7% annually via STRC dividends, distributed as monthly rebases) was compelling until you traced the dependency chain: STRC pays dividends from a company whose entire thesis is that Bitcoin goes up forever, which is either a feature or a ticking clock depending on your priors. A BVI-domiciled entity with a single-entity governance model, upgradeable proxy contracts, and a denylist controlled by ex-Uber and ex-Bird executives was not the typical stablecoin trust model, though monthly {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}} from The Network Firm added a layer of professional accountability. At roughly $2 million in circulation with 261 holders and negligible DEX volume, BUCK ended its life as a micro-cap experiment in whether you can build a savings product on top of someone else's Bitcoin maximalism.

bd-basedollar.title: Liquity's Fork, Aerodrome's Yield
bd-basedollar.text: BD is now live as Base's licensed Liquity V2 fork, with {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} borrowing against ETH, wstETH, rETH, cbETH, and cbBTC rather than the Aero LP collateral its pre-launch pitch emphasized. Stability Pool depositors collect borrower and liquidation fees, while AERO and Aerodrome LP branches remain the promised second act, a sensible sequence after the audit work found and fixed a high-severity LP-price manipulation flaw. The market has started narrowly: price discovery currently rests on one BD/USDC Aerodrome stableswap pool and circulation is still modest, so a dollar print is evidence of launch, not yet evidence of depth. The control model also lands between the branding and the bytecode: existing borrowing branches are collateral-gated and the token owner is renounced, but the collateral registry's 4-of-6 Safe can authorize new minting branches without a token-level cap or execution delay. That unbounded admin path is why economic control is the weakest of the three pillars on BD's {{grade}} card while backing and exit both read well, and it stays the binding question until the Aero flywheel is more than launch copy.

wm-m0.title: M Without the Yield
wm-m0.text: wM is M0's non-rebasing ERC-20 wrapper over M, backed by short-term U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} bills in bankruptcy-remote SPVs. The price of composability is that holders forfeit the yield. Underneath sits the same reserve framework and Validator {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} as M, while the wrapper routes accrued value to TTG-approved earner accounts through `claimExcess()`, leaving wM as a flat dollar for downstream integrations. Open wrap and unwrap keep the price anchored to M through arbitrage rather than a separate reserve operation, though Pharos records direct freeze reach because wrapper migration stays with an M0 migration admin Safe. Its multichain footprint makes wM the plumbing beneath a growing family of M0 extensions, with the yield living one layer further down. The durable constraint is structural: a wrapper cannot rate above its parent, so the {{grade}} overall grade is capped at M's own rating, and backing, inherited from M's collateral disclosure, is the weakest of the three pillars.

usdnr-nerona.title: Private Bank, Public Plumbing
usdnr-nerona.text: Nerona's USDnr is a thin permissioned wrapper over M0's $M, a tokenized short-term {{term:treasury}}T-bill{{/term}} exposure minted through MXON, with the T-bill carry accruing to the M0 reserve and Nerona rather than holders, who are pointed at the sUSDnr staking vault if they want the yield the marketing promises. The wrapper inherits every M0-layer risk: minter insolvency, governance deactivation, and real-time Validator attestations as the only reserve telemetry. All of it sits under single-entity governance with KYC-gated {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} reserved for clients of Nerona's private-wealth platform. Distribution has gone backwards: circulation peaked in the tens of millions in spring 2026 and has since collapsed by more than ninety percent to low-single-digit millions, which for a private-wealth product reads less like traction than a treasury parking spot being vacated. Mind the symbol: this is USDnr (Nerona, on Ethereum), not USDN (Noble's M0 wrapper on Cosmos). Sloppy press copy conflates the two, but they share nothing beyond the M0 plumbing underneath. A private bank for the onchain era, still waiting for depositors.

usdk-kast.title: The Anjouan Card Dollar
usdk-kast.text: KAST's USDK is an Anjouan-domiciled M0 wrapper of tokenized {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}, distributed through a fintech card app, with the T-bill yield retained by KAST rather than passed to holders. The token sits on Solana as a Token-2022 mint with permissioned transfer hooks and confidential-transfer extensions built in. This is useful if you trust KAST and BitGo, and awkward otherwise. At {{supplyUsd}} outstanding it is still proof-of-concept scale, riding entirely on M0 Validator {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}} rather than its own audit trail. Holders earn nothing; if you want the T-bill carry you're nudged into USDKy, KAST's separately rebasing twin. The legal stack is KAST Tech in Anjouan, {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} by partners, and a 'not a bank' disclaimer in bold. It is the modern offshore neobank uniform. A cleaner version of buying T-bills than most card-app stablecoins, provided you've made peace with single-jurisdiction issuer risk and a regulator most maps don't bother to label.

xo-exodus.title: Self-Custody's Custodial Dollar
xo-exodus.text: XO Cash is a MoonPay-issued dollar token on Solana, built as an M0 extension and distributed through the Exodus self-custody wallet and Exodus Pay. Every XO is backed by M held in the extension's vault, verified on-chain in September 2026 at just over full coverage, and M in turn is backed by short-term U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} bills held in bankruptcy-remote SPVs by M0's permissioned minters. The Token-2022 mint carries pausable, transfer-hook, and permanent-delegate controls held by MoonPay, so self-custody describes the wallet while the token's authorities stay with the issuer. Pharos scores economic control at the top of the scale on that verified structure, while backing is held down by what MoonPay does not publish: XO's current reserve custodians, provider allocation, and anti-rehypothecation terms. Exit is the weakest of the three pillars because the primary route is undisclosed and no comparable same-notional exit is on file; a child also cannot rate above its parent, so the {{grade}} overall grade sits under M's ceiling. The durable constraint is that XO borrows M0's reserve framework while leaving its own {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and exit terms undocumented.

sources.label: Exodus, MoonPay and M0 unveil a new digital dollar (press release)
M0 Dashboard: XO Cash powered by M0

jpysc-sbi-startale.title: Japan trust-bank JPY stablecoin
jpysc-sbi-startale.text: JPYSC went live on June 24, 2026 as Japan's first stablecoin issued through a trust bank rather than under JPYC's prepaid-instrument workaround, and that distinction is still the entire product. Shinsei Trust & Banking issues it, SBI VC Trade distributes it, and Startale Group built the rails; reserves sit as yen deposits in segregated trust-account {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} under FSA supervision, disclosed through trustee statutory filings rather than independent {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}. Its Type III electronic payment instrument classification gives JPYSC the trust-law {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} rights the prepaid model lacks, asset segregation, exemption from the ¥1M transfer cap, and permission to park up to 50% of reserves in {{term:treasury}}Japanese government bonds{{/term}}, which can generate yield that the prepaid model legally cannot touch. No cash-versus-JGB split has been published since launch, which is why backing is the weakest pillar on the card. The 'launch' remains a closed loop: only verified SBI VC Trade account holders can hold JPYSC, with no external-wallet withdrawals or public-chain circulation. Startale insists the on-chain plumbing is built and merely waiting on legal and tax clarity, not technology. Supply has roughly doubled since the June reserve disclosure, SBI VC Trade's lending product went live in July, and a DigiFT partnership is wiring JPYSC into tokenized capital-markets settlement, all with zero secondary-market volume because there is no secondary market. That is precisely the market-gating bet: Japan's stablecoin market was gated on legal infrastructure, and SBI's institutional book plus Startale's stack is designed to capture demand when the gate opens.

rgbp-revolut.title: Revolut Pre-Launch Sterling Stablecoin
rgbp-revolut.text:
Revolut's pre-launch UK GBP stablecoin remains sandbox-only, and the Bank of England rules once called structurally unviable have been substantially softened.

Revolut got its full UK banking licence in March 2026 after a 20-month mobilisation. It then confirmed its proposed GBP stablecoin would not be issued from the new banking entity, since BoE rules constrain issuing stablecoins across affiliated subsidiaries; issuance falls back to Revolut Ltd, the e-money arm. The regulatory weather has since turned: the BoE's June 2026 final policy statement scrapped the proposed £20,000 individual holding cap in favour of a temporary per-coin issuance ceiling of roughly £40bn, and lifted the share of reserves allowed in yield-bearing short-dated UK T-bills from 60% to 70%. This change retreated from exactly the provisions legal analysts had called commercially fatal. What survives is still austere: the remaining 30% sits unremunerated at the Bank, holders receive no yield, par {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} within 24 hours is mandatory, and the timeline runs through rules finalised by end-2026, regulated sterling coins from 2027, and full UK authorisation only in October 2027. The priority use case, per Revolut's House of Lords testimony, remains the UK→India remittance corridor, the world's seventh-largest, rather than retail payments. Revolut's real asset is its millions of UK users who already open the app daily, with bank-style {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and redemption bolted on top. The BoE no longer says the product cannot work; until its rules are final at end-2026, the sandbox is the only place the product exists.

sources.label: BoE policy statement and draft rules on systemic stablecoins (June 2026)
CoinDesk: BoE drops holding limits, sets $50bn issuance cap
Payment Expert: Revolut UK policy head on GBP stablecoin (House of Lords)

ausdt-tether-alloy.title: Gold Collateral, Dollar Target
ausdt-tether-alloy.text: aUSDT is Alloy by Tether's dollar stablecoin: a {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} where verified users deposit Tether Gold (XAUT) and mint dollars at up to 75% LTV, so the peg sits on top of {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} gold rather than a bank account. Alloy Tether turns Tether Gold into a dollar-tracking credit instrument: verified users deposit XAUT into an Ethereum vault, mint aUSDT against a 75% mint-to-value ceiling, and return aUSDT plus fees to withdraw collateral. That gives Pharos a clean on-chain reserve view because the XAUT backing sits in the CMPVault, but it also means aUSDT inherits Tether Gold {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, gold-price volatility, whitelist access, and {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} mechanics. The peg rests on an overcollateralized gold position engineered to trade near one dollar, not on a bank-account promise. It is also now a position in run-off: Tether is winding down the Alloy platform, new minting is halted, and holders have until mid-September 2026 to return aUSDT and pull their XAUT collateral before the exit window closes. The experiment ends as a footnote to Tether's gold strategy: the market wanted the bullion token, not a dollar derivative of it.

usdsui-sui.title: Sui Gets Its Native Dollar
usdsui-sui.text: USDsui is Sui's native dollar, issued through Bridge, Stripe's stablecoin infrastructure arm, as a fiat-backed alternative to another {{term:bridge}}bridged{{/term}} dollar. The reserve model is conventional Bridge Open Issuance: cash, short-dated {{term:treasury}}Treasuries{{/term}}, repos, and government {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market funds{{/term}} in segregated accounts support mint and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}, with institutional {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} at Lead Bank, BlackRock, and Fidelity. Bridge's public transparency endpoint now reports a USDsui-specific split of roughly nine-tenths Treasuries and one-tenth cash, but it is self-reported with no independent {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} and no publication cadence. That is why backing is the weakest of the three pillars on the {{grade}} card: the disclosed composition is clean, the assurance behind it is thin. Redemption runs through Bridge for eligible customers, minting is issuer-controlled and reconciled against reserves, and the primary exit is eligibility-gated. USDsui gives Sui a native dollar, and the card will move only when the reserve evidence moves beyond the issuer's own word.

brlv-crown.title: Brazilian Bonds On Chain
brlv-crown.text: BRLV is Crown's centralized Brazilian real stablecoin, minted and redeemed 1:1 for BRL by KYC'd users and backed almost entirely by Brazilian federal government bonds pledged to token holders through a security-agent structure in segregated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. That is a cleaner reserve story than most emerging-market fiat coins: the backing is local sovereign debt rather than offshore dollar liquidity, and the legal structure is designed to keep reserve claims separate from Crown itself. The risks are equally specific: BRL liquidity, Brazilian sovereign-rate volatility, and KYC-gated {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}. The evidence has limits too. Monthly reserve memos come from Fact Finance, an oracle firm signing as a technical lead rather than an accountant, so the reports carry no assurance opinion, and the custodians behind the segregation claim are not named. Native issuance is on Base, with an issuer-relayed representation on Ethereum. On the {{grade}} card the exit pillar is the weakest of the three, since primary exit is eligibility-gated and that gate is the route Pharos scores.

sources.label: Crown BRLV transparency and monthly reports

usdglo-glo.title: Glo Dollar Public-Goods Reserve
usdglo-glo.text: Glo Dollar is Brale-issued dollar plumbing with an unusual allocation decision: reserve yield funds public-goods causes instead of being rebated to holders, exchanges, or the issuer's distribution partners. The backing itself is deliberately ordinary, split between cash-like assets and U.S. government-backed debt, with monthly management reports that carry no accountant's opinion and 1:1 mint and redemption through Brale. That makes USDGLO's differentiation moral and distributional, not mechanical, which is more interesting than another fake innovation label. Pharos also tracks it because small stablecoins can still become meaningful dependencies when they show up inside other reserve stacks. The report card scores the evidence gap rather than the reserve mix: backing is the weakest of the three pillars because the reports name no banks, custodians, or instruments behind the cash and government-debt lines, while the exit pillar leads the card on seven issuer-native deployments and direct redemption. USDGLO redirects the float rather than out-engineering Circle, which is both noble and commercially inconvenient.

usdon-ondo.title: Ondo Settlement Cash
usdon-ondo.text: USDon is the cash leg inside Ondo Global Markets, used to settle purchases and redemptions of tokenized assets under Ondo's platform structure. Ondo states it is backed one-for-one by U.S. dollar cash or cash equivalents in brokerage accounts, but no USDon-specific reserve report, broker identity, or instrument mix is published, so the backing pillar carries a missing-composition cap and limited evidence. Access is whitelisted, the platform dependency is total, and issuer-admin controls keep the risk model institutional. Pharos treats {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} as a Global Markets route gated by eligibility rather than a permissionless on-chain backstop, and that gated exit is the weakest of the three pillars on the {{grade}} card. USDon is settlement cash with a ticker; its value to a holder ends at the platform boundary.

audm-macropod.title: Australia's New On-Chain Dollar
audm-macropod.text: AUDM is Macropod's institutional Australian dollar: approved clients deposit AUD into a trustee-held reserve, Macropod mints against it, and redemption runs back through the same narrow channel. The paper trail is fuller than the float suggests: a quarterly Hall Chadwick agreed-upon-procedures engagement sits alongside monthly issuer self-verification reports, and the latest self-report reconciles AUD cash held at Westpac by Macropod as trustee for the AUDM Trust against on-chain supply across four networks to within a rounding error. Read the engagement before celebrating it: the procedures express no opinion and the report notes the firm was not required to be independent, so the engagement covers arithmetic rather than any assurance that the arrangement is sound. Backing is nonetheless the weakest of the three pillars on the {{grade}} card. For a float this small, quarterly no-opinion procedures are a reasonable place to start and a poor place to settle. The constraints remain scale and cadence: the mint is economically unbounded and reconciled only after the fact, and the track record is still short.

audf-forte.title: Audited Cash, No Established Exit
audf-forte.text: AUDF is Forte Securities Australia's centralized Australian dollar stablecoin, issued under an ASIC AFSL and described as redeemable 1:1 for AUD held in a segregated reserve bank account. The strongest verified fact is the reserve report: Horizon Nexus audited a single segregated, unencumbered AUD bank-account balance as at 31 May 2026, but the bank is unnamed, the report reconciles no liabilities, and no newer report had been published by late August, so the composition has aged past Pharos's freshness window and the card carries a missing-composition ceiling. The exit line is the problem. Forte's Terms of Use state that holders have no entitlement to the reserves, no security interest, and no trust or fiduciary relationship, and Pharos has not established a viable exit path, which is why the exit pillar is the weakest of the three and the {{grade}} overall grade sits where it does despite a peg history with very few recorded episodes. Economic control fares better: a 2-of-5 admin Safe holds mint and upgrade authority across five issuer-native deployments. With a reserve of a few million Australian dollars at the last audit, AUDF is not systemically important, and the durable constraint is that a clean audit of cash says nothing about whether a holder can compel {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}.

sources.label: AUDF Reserves Report and Horizon Nexus independent auditor's report (31 May 2026 reserve date; signed 16 June 2026)

busd0-usual.title: Fixed-Maturity USD0 Bond
busd0-usual.text: bUSD0 is Usual's bond-leg wrapper of USD0, formerly USD0++, renamed under the UIP-12 redesign: a fixed-notional bond maturing June 11, 2028 that behaves like a discount instrument, not a spot dollar, before that date. Par {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} before maturity requires pairing bUSD0 with the separately tradeable rt-bUSD0 early-exit right, while standalone bUSD0 can trade below one dollar; yield arrives as daily USUAL token coupons rather than dollar NAV growth, so holders stack USD0 reserve quality, Usual DAO parameter risk, and pre-maturity discount risk. The product keeps evolving around its holders: the Usual Stability Loan that lets bUSD0 collateralize USD0 borrowing migrated from Euler to Fira in January 2026, and the underlying USD0 claim remains an {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} stack. Pharos has held the listing in quarantine since mid-July 2026 because none of its permitted market-data sources report a positive circulating supply or market cap: a fitting limbo for a bond that renamed itself out of the stablecoin category, only for the data feeds to agree it is not quite a dollar.

susde-ethena.title: Ethena's Savings Sleeve
susde-ethena.text: sUSDe is the yield wrapper over USDe, converting Ethena staking rewards into a rising exchange rate rather than a separate payout. Economically it inherits the same USDe reserve and custody stack: liquid stablecoin backing, delta-neutral BTC and ETH/LST hedges, off-exchange custody, CEX execution, and the operational choreography that keeps the synthetic dollar flat. The wrapper's separate risk is exit timing, because unstaking burns the receipt immediately while the holder still waits through Ethena's seven-day cooldown before receiving liquid USDe. Pharos therefore treats sUSDe as a wrapper dependency that carries the parent risk in full. Exit is the weakest of the three pillars because of that cooldown, and the {{grade}} overall grade is capped at the parent USDe score. It is USDe with yield accounting and a waiting room; the waiting room is the constraint.

susds-sky.title: The Plain Sky Savings Token
susds-sky.text: sUSDS is the plain savings receipt in the Sky stack: deposit USDS, receive an ERC-4626-style token whose exchange rate compounds with the Sky Savings Rate. That simplicity is the point, especially next to stUSDS, which pushes holders into risk-capital exposure and borrower shortfall risk. The wrapper still inherits the USDS reserve mix, Sky governance, and the USDS PSM exit surface, so it stays attached to the parent system even though the vault interface is clean. Pharos reads sUSDS as the clean yield-bearing expression of Sky's base dollar rather than a separate reserve design. Exit leads the card, since USDS is withdrawable directly from the vault with no fee. Economic control is the weakest of the three pillars: the vault is a ward-gated UUPS proxy, and the Base, Optimism, and Arbitrum representations sit behind administered SkyLink bridges. The {{grade}} overall grade is capped at the parent USDS score, which is the durable ceiling for any wrapper in this stack.

sdai-sky.title: The Classic DSR Wrapper
sdai-sky.text: sDAI is the original Dai savings receipt: deposit DAI and receive a token whose redeemable DAI balance grows with the Dai Savings Rate. It adds very little conceptual complexity beyond the base asset, but it still belongs on its own row because holders are choosing a NAV-appreciating {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} wrapper with its own liquidity, integrations, and wrapper-contract risk rather than plain DAI. The underlying still inherits DAI's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} collateral profile. The Ethereum wrapper is a non-upgradeable contract with no owner, pause, or blacklist function, and almost all supply sits there rather than on the Base and OP Mainnet bridge representations, so the {{grade}} overall grade is capped at the parent DAI rating rather than by any wrapper finding.

sfrxusd-frax.title: Frax's Yield Sleeve
sfrxusd-frax.text: sfrxUSD is the savings sleeve for frxUSD rather than a second Frax dollar with its own reserve book. Depositors trade the flat base token for a vault share whose exchange rate rises as Frax routes frxUSD income and custodian yield into the wrapper. That distinction matters: wrapper risk is share accounting, redemption mechanics, and liquidity for sfrxUSD, while the parent stablecoin risk remains the frxUSD custodian and reserve stack. The multichain footprint makes the token easier to hold, but it also turns a simple Treasury-style reserve story into Frax governance, issuer controls, and bridge-aware exit math. The live Ethereum implementation exposes an authorized minter path with no token-level amount cap, twenty-eight of thirty deployments are LayerZero OFT representations whose validation configuration remains unresolved, and no comparable exit route is documented. Economic control is the weakest of the three pillars and exit is next, so the {{grade}} overall grade sits below the parent frxUSD rating even though backing is the strong line.

scrvusd-curve.title: Borrower Interest Receipt
scrvusd-curve.text: scrvUSD is Curve's ERC-4626 savings share over crvUSD, so the wrapper adds yield and exchange-rate behavior without inventing a new dollar. Deposited crvUSD backs the share, while borrower interest and protocol revenue make the redeemable crvUSD balance climb over time. The wrapper risk is vault accounting, liquidity, and the ability to exit back into crvUSD; the parent risk is still Curve's CDP and LLAMMA machinery, with BTC and ETH collateral doing the heavy lifting underneath. Holding scrvUSD is cleaner than holding raw crvUSD, but it stays tied to the machinery that mints the base asset, and the {{grade}} overall grade is capped at the parent crvUSD rating.

cusdo-openeden.title: Non-Rebasing OpenDollar
cusdo-openeden.text: cUSDO is OpenEden's non-rebasing wrapper for USDO, built for protocols that would rather watch a price rise than reconcile changing balances. It keeps the same underlying OpenDollar claim: tokenized {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} exposure and issuer-controlled {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} rails, but moves the yield expression into NAV appreciation. That makes the product mechanically useful without making the reserve chain any shorter: cUSDO still depends on USDO, OpenEden, and the underlying tokenized T-bill stack. Its {{grade}} overall grade is borrowed rather than earned: a child cannot rate above its required parent, so cUSDO's ceiling is USDO's score, and nothing about the wrapper itself moves it. Backing is the weakest pillar on the card for exactly that inherited reason, while exit and economic control both grade near the top. The wrapper's own admin surface is issuer-held upgrade and pause authority across its deployments, plus a Solana signer that holds both mint and freeze power, so composability does not equal neutrality. cUSDO is a formatting layer over the same dollar claim, and its safety can never exceed that claim's.

syusd-aegis.title: Aegis Cooldown Wrapper
syusd-aegis.text: sYUSD is Aegis's staking wrapper over YUSD, capitalizing funding-rate income into a rising exchange rate instead of paying out a separate coupon. The parent stablecoin risk is YUSD's BTC spot plus short-perpetual hedge model and off-exchange custody assumptions; the wrapper risk is the ERC-4626 vault, its upgradeable proxy under a 3-of-5 Safe, and the seven-day cooldown before holders get back to liquid YUSD. Accountable provides real-time reserve visibility, which is useful, but it does not turn a delta-neutral basis trade into a bank deposit. Backing is the weakest of the three pillars because it is YUSD's backing seen through a wrapper, and the {{grade}} overall grade is capped at the parent YUSD score. The product is different enough from YUSD to deserve its own row and similar enough that the two cards cannot move independently.

stusds-sky.title: Sky Risk-Capital USDS
stusds-sky.text: stUSDS is Sky's expert-mode risk-capital module over USDS: deposited USDS funds SKY-backed borrowing while idle liquidity earns the Sky Savings Rate, exposing holders to borrower shortfall, governance slashing, utilization, and withdrawal-liquidity risk. As a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} module distinct from passive {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} paths, it inherits the broad Sky/USDS ecosystem and ranks differently from USDS and sUSDS because its value can be affected by staked-SKY loan performance. The {{grade}} overall grade is capped at the parent USDS score, and backing is the weakest of the three pillars because the reserve is one SKY-collateralized loan receivable rather than a diversified cash position.

stcusd-cap.title: Cap Yield Wrapper
stcusd-cap.text: stcUSD is the {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} version of Cap cUSD: users stake cUSD into an ERC-4626 vault while Cap operators borrow reserve assets against restaker collateral and repay with yield above the hurdle rate. Cap's design attempts to keep stablecoin holders whole through {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} and slashing, but stcUSD still adds operator, restaker, strategy, and vault risk on top of the underlying cUSD basket and its {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} mechanics. The wrapper has no separate privileged mint path and its upgrade authority sits behind a one-day timelock and Cap's governance Safe, so the {{grade}} overall grade is capped at the parent cUSD rating rather than by a wrapper-specific finding.

said-gaib.title: AI Infrastructure NAV Token
said-gaib.text: sAID is GAIB's staked AID vault token, and it floats with the NAV of AI infrastructure financing positions rather than holding AID's stable base. AID is intended as the base currency backed by {{term:treasury}}Treasuries{{/term}} and accepted stablecoins; sAID layers a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} wrapper over a private credit book of AI infrastructure financings plus stable reserve buffers. Monthly withdrawal cycles, unrealized-loss-aware unstaking NAV, and private AI financing exposure make it a materially different asset from AID. Pharos scores that difference directly: backing is the weakest of the three pillars, and the {{grade}} overall grade cannot rise above the parent AID rating.

msy-main-street.title: Death by Parent
msy-main-street.text: msY was Main Street's ERC-4626-style {{term:yield-bearing}}yield share{{/term}} over msUSD, accruing value from the protocol's options and derivatives strategy while final exit ran back through msUSD's capacity-managed USDC {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}. That layering stopped being theoretical on June 20, 2026: reserve verifier Accountable terminated its contract over inadequate proof of reserves, msUSD collapsed to cents on the dollar, and the vault share, with no independent backing of its own, followed the parent down. The unwind also jammed the side exits, with the Morpho msY/USDC lending market pinned at full utilization while roughly $18 million sat trapped inside. Pharos now carries msY as frozen, a derivative casualty of counterparty failure rather than an active dollar instrument. The original risk disclosure covered strategy, {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, and liquidity risk stacked on top of base redemption. That turned out to be the whole story, except the base redemption never showed up.

yusd-yieldfi.title: YieldFi USDC Strategy Vault
yusd-yieldfi.text: YieldFi's yUSD is an ERC-4626 share over USDC that its manager routes into Pendle principal tokens, Morpho and Silo vaults, private credit, and hedged carry. The manager makes discretionary allocations while the product is priced as a dollar. Its backing pillar scores near the top of the scale, and that is reliably the least informative figure on the card: what backs yUSD on paper is USDC, while what determines whether it holds a dollar is allocator judgement and the exit terms of venues under no obligation to be liquid on your schedule. The {{grade}} overall grade was never coming from the reserve. Economic control sits at the floor for a concrete reason: alongside deposit-minted shares, the manager holds a discretionary mint-and-burn path with no supply ceiling, gated on roles that two externally owned accounts can grant or revoke instantly. Add an exit pillar with no comparable same-notional route out, the weakest line on the card, and the overall grade follows. Pharos tracks this apart from Aegis YUSD and YO Protocol's yoUSD because the name collision conceals a different issuer and a very different risk.

sbold-k3-capital.title: K3 Stability Pool BOLD
sbold-k3-capital.text: sBOLD is K3 Capital's ERC-4626 wrapper around BOLD deposited into Liquity V2 Stability Pools. It earns interest and {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} gains while automating the conversion of liquidated ETH and LST collateral back into BOLD. The base BOLD system is immutable and fully on-chain with {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-based issuance, but sBOLD adds K3-controlled vault, oracle, solver, and fee-switch risk, so it belongs as a separate wrapper exposure. The wrapper itself is a non-upgradeable contract with no holder freeze path, and its {{grade}} overall grade is capped at the parent BOLD rating rather than by any wrapper-specific finding.

ybold-yearn.title: Yearn's BOLD Stability Pool Vault
ybold-yearn.text: yBOLD is Yearn's ERC-4626 wrapper around BOLD deposited into Liquity V2 Stability Pool strategies, layering vault and strategy risk onto Liquity's CDP-redemption design. It is a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} wrapper that auto-compounds {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} rewards from Liquity's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} system. It keeps the economic exposure anchored to BOLD while automating allocation across Stability Pools and liquidation-reward compounding through Yearn-managed strategy contracts. Holders can {{term:redemption}}redeem{{/term}} the vault share back into BOLD at the live exchange rate, but the exposure is not the same as holding base BOLD: it adds Yearn vault governance, strategy execution, auction, and smart-contract risk on top of Liquity's collateral-redemption design. The {{grade}} overall grade is a ceiling set by BOLD itself: a wrapper cannot rate above the asset it requires, so every pillar on the card scores above the grade the card is allowed to carry.

stkgho-umbrella-aave.title: Aave Umbrella GHO Staking
stkgho-umbrella-aave.text: Aave Umbrella stkGHO is a slashable staking receipt over GHO, which made it much more interesting than a passive savings wrapper and much less comfortable to hold during a deficit event. Depositors earn Umbrella rewards, but they also accept cooldowns, withdrawal windows, and automated loss absorption if covered GHO shortfalls materialize. Durable GHO issuance still inherits Aave's facilitator and governance controls underneath. Pharos therefore treats stkGHO as a risk-absorption asset, not a cleaner version of the base CDP stablecoin, with the non-slashable sGHO vault as the designated savings lane for anyone who never wanted the insurance job. That job is now being retired: a late-June governance vote approved sunsetting the GHO Umbrella market. Emissions and target liquidity wound to zero, the deficit offset padded so existing stakers can exit in order, and future GHO shortfalls handed to the DAO treasury instead. The yield here was payment for being useful when something goes wrong, and Aave has concluded it no longer needs to outsource that usefulness. That leaves stkGHO as a receipt for a risk the protocol is taking back in-house.

sources.label: Aave governance: Umbrella Parameter Update ARFC (GHO Umbrella sunset)
Aave Umbrella documentation (sGHO and Umbrella staking)

myrc-blox.title: Assurance Found, Composition Expired
myrc-blox.text: MYRC is Malaysia's first ringgit stablecoin, issued by Blox and gated through MyKad eKYC to Malaysian residents with a linked local bank account, a deliberately small, deliberately domestic product with a float in the low millions of ringgit. This release moves it in two opposite directions at once. A verification pass found what an earlier one had missed: Tommy Ung & Partners PLT really are issuing monthly ISAE 3000 reasonable-assurance opinions that MYR assets held equal or exceed MYRC in circulation, a recurring third-party reconciliation of the strongest kind short of a full audit, which lifts economic control off the floor and the card to its current {{grade}}. But the same June examination re-anchored the composition date, pushing the reserve split, mostly ringgit bank cash with the remainder in a Shariah-compliant {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market fund{{/term}}, outside the 31-day freshness window, so backing is now scored against no admitted composition at all and a missing-composition ceiling binds the card. The irony is exact: the report that proved the reserves are real is too old to describe them. Blox still holds no Bank Negara or Securities Commission licence and its own term sheet concedes MYRC is not electronic money, so the auditor is doing all of the supervisory work here.

krwq-iq.title: Korean Won Stablecoin, Still Dollar-Backed
krwq-iq.text: KRWQ is the first stablecoin pegged 1:1 to the South Korean won, launched October 2025 by IQ in partnership with Frax, with KYC-gated institutional access and a reserve that still sits in dollar stablecoins rather than the Korean government bonds it targets. It uses LayerZero's Omnichain Fungible Token (OFT) standard with Ethereum as the canonical mint chain and Base as the primary bridged destination, sharing unified supply across deployments. The stated reserve target is a mix dominated by short-term Korean Treasury Bonds tokenized through Etherfuse's Stablebond framework and held in segregated, bankruptcy-remote custody at Shinhan Securities. The issuer's live reserve feed, however, reports frxUSD as the bulk of reserves, USDC for the remainder, and no Korean Treasury Bond exposure at all. Mint and redemption are KYC-gated to institutional counterparties (exchanges, market makers, OTC desks), and KRWQ is explicitly not marketed to South Korean residents while domestic stablecoin legislation moves through the National Assembly. That gated primary market is why exit is the weakest pillar on the card. The transparency stack took a real step in June when KRWQ was wired into Chainlink Proof of Reserve for automated verification, though the promised independent monthly attestations still lack a named auditor. The Shinhan Securities {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} applies only to the Korean {{term:treasury}}treasury bond{{/term}} slice, which the feed currently reports at zero, so holders today carry Frax and Circle counterparty risk behind KYC-gated {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} and a LayerZero OFT {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}}.

reur-royal-euro.title: Delisted Into the Dark
reur-royal-euro.text:
A delisted euro token from RIB Digital Holdings whose public markets vanished and whose self-reported reserve snapshots stalled months earlier.

Pharos no longer tracks REUR as an active stablecoin: AscendEX delisted its only identified public markets at the end of June 2026, and the issuer now describes access through approved institutional, OTC, and private settlement channels. There is no ordinary public route to acquire or redeem this euro. Transparency decayed in parallel: the self-signed proof-of-reserves snapshots, pitched as near-real-time, stalled in late April 2026 and have not been updated since. What remains is a Hong Kong-domiciled euro claim on issuer-managed bank deposits, with self-reported reserves and discretionary {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} terms doing all the load-bearing work. A stablecoin you cannot publicly buy, verify, or exit is a private IOU wearing a ticker.

sources.label: AscendEX RUSD and REUR delisting notice
RIB Digital transparency page (snapshot series stalled April 2026)

kgst-kyrgyz-som.title: Central Asia's On-Chain Som
kgst-kyrgyz-som.text: KGST is a Kyrgyz som stablecoin on BNB Chain tracked by CoinGecko, presented as a fully backed 1:1 KGS token with bank reserves and no verified attestation cadence. It gives Pharos a direct Central Asian local-currency peg, but public reserve and redemption materials remain limited compared with established regulated fiat issuers, and the issuer site names neither the banks nor a dated reserve balance. KGST also depends on secondary FX feeds for USD normalization because CoinGecko does not currently expose a native KGS quote. On-chain, minting is uncapped and sits with a 2-of-5 Safe that also owns the proxy admin, with no timelock, and the same owner can freeze individual holders or pause the token. Without a verified cadence of {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, transparent {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, or a documented {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} window, the issuer's 1:1 claim remains unaudited by Pharos, and missing evidence is recorded as undisclosed rather than read as safety.

audx-aussie-dollar-token.title: Assured AUD Cash, Narrow Exit
audx-aussie-dollar-token.text: AUDX is the centralized Australian dollar stablecoin of TAU Pty Ltd, trading as AUDX Token, designed for 1:1 AUD {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}, backed by AUD cash and government-backed instruments, and tracked across Ethereum, Polygon, Conflux, and XDC. The issuer describes AUSTRAC registration and 1:1 AUD reserves held in regulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} at financial institutions, and Aura Partners now publishes monthly limited-assurance reports under ASAE 3000 and 3100 that confirm designated reserve balances directly with the banks and reconcile them to issued supply, though the banks are not named and the firm shares a Sydney floor with the issuer. That evidence carries the backing line; the exit pillar is the weakest of the three on the {{grade}} card, since primary redemption is eligibility-gated and market depth is still small. Pharos treats the reserve story as verified but the exit as less battle-tested than older AUD rails with longer public operating histories.

sources.label: Aura Partners AUDX Independent Limited Assurance Report - July 2026

cngn-compliant-naira.title: Naira Settlement Goes Multichain
cngn-compliant-naira.text: cNGN is a Nigerian naira stablecoin built as regulated settlement infrastructure rather than a dollar substitute, issued natively on Bantu and distributed to eight tracked networks through the issuer's lock-and-mint bridge. The reserve claim is 1:1 naira in accounts at licensed Nigerian commercial banks, and that is where the evidence stops: the transparency page names no bank, publishes no allocation, and links no dated reserve examination, while the monthly audit the issuer describes has no reachable report. The regulatory anchor is a Nigerian SEC approval-in-principle under its Accelerated Regulatory Incubation Programme; a final licence has not been granted. The {{grade}} overall grade reflects all three pillars sitting at the bottom of the scale, with economic control the weakest: the Bantu issuer account carries no economic cap or timelock, no whole-supply reconciliation covers the destination representations, and the upgrade authority on several of them is unresolved. The peg record has also turned: after a clean first year, a single-source quote pushed cNGN materially below par in July 2026, and Pharos was still flagging that episode as open in early September. The multichain footprint improves utility for payments and exchange settlement, but until the banks, balances, and reconciliation are published, compliant naira rails remain a promise Pharos cannot verify.

brl1-brl1.title: A Consortium-Issued Real
brl1-brl1.text: BRL1 is a centralized Brazilian real stablecoin on Polygon, issued by BRL1 CONSORTIUM S.A. and targeting a 1:1 peg with a reserve mix of Brazilian federal LFT bonds, repurchase agreements, and a BRL bank balance, all reported in a segregated account at Banco XP. It adds another BRL-denominated route alongside the older Brazilian real tokens in Pharos, but with a smaller operating footprint and thinner disclosure than the most established local issuers: the reserve report is prepared internally, board-approved, and explicitly not audited, and there is no regular third-party {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}. Pharos verified the report's stated liability against the Polygon supply at the report block, which checks the token count but not the off-chain balances. The {{grade}} overall grade is held down less by backing than by economic control, the weakest of the three pillars: a single EOA holds the only minter role with no supply cap, and another EOA can grant minting or upgrade rights immediately. The repo counterparty and the individual securities are undisclosed, so the reserve story stays issuer-asserted.

wars-argentine-peso.title: Ripio's Peso Token on a Single Certification
wars-argentine-peso.text: WARS is the Argentine peso token in Ripio's wFIAT suite, issued natively on Ethereum, Base, World Chain, BNB Chain, Polygon, and Gnosis at one deterministic address, with a Celo deployment tracked separately, and moved between chains by Ripio's own burn-and-mint {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}} rail rather than an external validator set. The reserve evidence is a single certification: an independent Argentine accountant reconciled roughly 973 million outstanding wARS to about ARS 1.04 billion of deposits at unnamed Argentine financial institutions as of 31 March 2026, in an engagement that expressly is not an audit and expresses no opinion. Pharos probed for later monthly certifications through July and found none, so the composition is stale under v9 and the {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} chain, provider allocations, and failure mechanics remain undisclosed. One issuer key holds mint, upgrade, and pause roles on every deployment, which the card scores as concentrated but reconciled control. Backing and exit are the weak pillars, and the overall line currently reads {{grade}}. {{term:redemption}}Redemption{{/term}} confidence therefore rests on Ripio's off-ramp, not on anything a holder can verify on-chain.

sources.label: Independent public accountant certification for wARS - March 2026

pusd-polymarket.title: The Prediction-Market Wrapper
pusd-polymarket.text: Polymarket USD is the application-tier dollar balance token used around Polymarket deposits and withdrawals on Polygon, mapped to USDC and USDC.e rather than to a new reserve. Its collateral story is simple: the token wraps USDC held in one identified backing vault, so reserve risk is mostly wrapper, {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}}, and app-access risk rather than a new asset mix. Pharos validates the vault balances against the Polygon contract and keeps the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path documented through Polymarket docs. The {{grade}} overall grade leans on the exit pillar, the strongest line on the card, because unwrapping to USDC is permissionless and immediate; backing is the weakest of the three because the claim is a pass-through on USDC held in a protocol vault, with Circle's freeze reach inherited. The token itself has no blacklist or holder-freeze path, though a Safe-controlled timelock can replace its logic, and Polymarket's official Bridge API remains an undisclosed cross-chain route. Launched in April 2026, the token still sits under a track-record ceiling. The token functions as an application dollar whose risk lives in Polymarket's rails.

rusd-royal-dollar.title: Private Settlement Only
rusd-royal-dollar.text:
A delisted Royal/R Coins dollar whose reserve questions were never answered before its public markets disappeared.

Royal Dollar is no longer tracked as an active stablecoin: AscendEX delisted the only identified public RUSD markets at the end of June 2026, and the issuer now describes access through approved institutional, OTC, and private settlement channels. No ordinary public acquisition or redemption route remains. The transparency questions that dogged the token while listed were never resolved on the way out. The issuer's reserve snapshot dated 23 April 2026 classified the backing as cash and bank deposits without naming the deposit banks or their liquidity terms, and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} mechanics stayed too opaque to model as a high-quality fiat backstop. Pharos's reserve validation was limited to confirming tracked on-chain supply against a curated view. The Hong Kong-domiciled issuer's discretionary redemption terms and KYC-gated processes now operate entirely out of public sight, alongside sister token REUR, which exited through the same door on the same day. A dollar claim that leaves the public market before publishing a real {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} is not a stablecoin story that gets a second act.

sources.label: AscendEX RUSD and REUR delisting notice

usdr-ring.title: The Ring Protocol Dollar
usdr-ring.text: Ring Protocol's USDR is a small Ethereum dollar whose backing is undisclosed. Ring's current documentation covers its swap and token tooling but publishes no USDR reserve inventory, and the verified token contract is a role-gated mint-and-burn ERC-20 with no reserve ledger, bonding curve, or holder {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} function. The launch transaction minted the initial supply directly to a minter address with no collateral argument, and four minters can still mint to any address without a cap. Pharos therefore records the reserve stack as a single undisclosed position and does not model a redemption backstop. On the {{grade}} card, backing and economic control are the two weakest pillars while the exit pillar leads, because secondary-market exit routes exist even though they share a failure domain. USDR is a long-tail dollar whose peg rests on issuer discretion and protocol liquidity rather than any documented reserve.

uusd-anything-labs.title: The BSC Unity Dollar
uusd-anything-labs.text: Unity USD is Anything Labs's issuer-controlled dollar token on BNB Chain, and its defining feature is what is not published. Pharos re-opened the website, whitepaper, and contract repository in July 2026 and found no disclosure of reserve assets, custodians, {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} rails, or any reserve {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}; the whitepaper is a conceptual AI-settlement essay with no reserve section, and DefiLlama's line that UUSD is backed by USDT and USDC is not corroborated by any issuer primary. On-chain the token is an upgradeable proxy whose owner Safe can mint and burn directly, freeze any address, and pause all transfers, with the same Safe controlling the upgrade path. The peg has held near par on thin, low-confidence pricing, which says little given that no mechanism for maintaining it is described. All three pillars sit at the floor of the card, so the {{grade}} overall grade reflects absence of evidence rather than a measured failure. Until Anything Labs publishes what stands behind the token, UUSD is a supply figure with an owner key and nothing verifiable underneath.

jusd-jusd-stable-token.title: The Small Multichain Dollar
jusd-jusd-stable-token.text: JUSD is a long-tail dollar token with BSC and Polygon contracts, issuer/protocol-managed crypto collateral, and an unverified reserve composition. Pharos models its reserves as protocol-managed crypto collateral because public materials do not provide a reviewed, granular collateral breakdown: the 2023 whitepaper describes a diversified reserve but names no assets, custodians, or amounts and publishes no attestation. Canonical issuance sits on Polygon, where an owner EOA can call an uncapped mint, while the BSC deployment is a Chainport bridge representation; Pharos reads the BSC contract for curated validation and keeps Polygon for discovery. The main risk is the limited transparency around reserve composition and live redemption depth. Since mid-July 2026 Pharos has held JUSD in quarantine because no permitted runtime source reports a positive circulating supply or market cap. Until JUSD publishes a third-party {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} and discloses {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop and reserve quality remain unmodelled by Pharos.

jusd-juicedollar.title: Juice Dollar Wind-Down
jusd-juicedollar.text: Juice Dollar was a Citrea-native USD stablecoin built on the Frankencoin and d-EURO architecture: oracle-free {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} positions collateralized by wrapped cBTC, permissionless challenge auctions standing in for a price feed at {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}}, and an ownerless accepted-minter registry with no admin key. In practice the bitcoin path was barely used. Pharos's July 2026 review of the issuer API and Citrea RPC found zero WCBTC held across all positions and roughly 56,700 JUSD outstanding, almost all of it minted 1:1 through the StablecoinBridge against bridged USDT.e, so the token was in effect a wrapper on bridged Tether with Tether's freeze power sitting on the reserve. The project announced a wind-down on 6 August 2026, and Pharos delisted JUSD on 10 August after {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} ended, issuer control was lost, the website and app were permanently shut down, and a new uncontrolled minter became active on-chain. In this design an accepted minter can mint an unrestricted amount and the contracts are immutable and ownerless, so the shutdown notice is the issuer's last word and the open mint is the record's durable fact.

usda-alpha-partner.title: The Alpha Partner Dollar
usda-alpha-partner.text: Alpha Partner USDA is a BSC-only dollar token with more ambition than disclosure, which is a familiar ratio in the long tail. The issuer describes protocol-managed collateral and liquidity reserves, but the metadata still has no credible reserve composition, no independent attestation, and no documented mint or redemption mechanics beyond a role-gated token contract. Pharos can validate the tracked on-chain supply and record the blacklistable, admin-heavy control surface; it cannot turn vague collateral language into a clean backstop. The FDIC-style claims that circulate on aggregator listings are especially unhelpful, because stablecoin reserves do not become insured by borrowing bank vocabulary, and a July 2026 re-read of the issuer's own website and documentation found no mention of USDA at all. The peg record shows a long tail of episodes below par. Every pillar on the card sits at the bottom of the scale behind the {{grade}} overall grade, and the confidence level should stay low until the issuer publishes something less ornamental.

xdai-gnosis.title: The Native Gnosis Dollar
xdai-gnosis.text: xDAI is the native gas token of Gnosis Chain, credited only when the canonical xDAI bridge escrows USDS on Ethereum, so its peg quality cascades from Sky and from Gnosis bridge infrastructure. Unlike a normal ERC-20 stablecoin, its canonical supply is native-chain accounting, so Pharos lists the WXDAI wrapper as a traded contract rather than using it as the supply contract. The reserve view is a {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}} escrow: after the completed migration from DAI, the Foreign Bridge holds almost all of its collateral as sUSDS, Sky's savings vault, with a small liquid USDS buffer, and pinned reads reconcile that escrow to bridge-minted-minus-burnt xDAI with a slight surplus. Peg quality therefore depends on Sky's USDS, itself a {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-backed dollar, on the sUSDS vault's liquidity, and on a 4-of-7 validator set and 8-of-15 admin Safes with no contract-enforced timelock. Native balances carry no local freeze, but a Sky-side freeze could impair the escrow and the exit path, which is why exit is the weakest of the three pillars on the card. It is more infrastructure dollar than issuer token.

sources.label: Gnosis xDAI bridge USDS migration specification at commit 52afd25

usdx-kava.title: The Legacy Kava Debt Dollar
usdx-kava.text: Kava USDX is the legacy Kava Mint {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} debt token, backed by crypto collateral and {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} mechanics, and it trades at a deep discount to the dollar; Pharos keeps it in the catalog as a live depeg case rather than a healthy par dollar. The live CDP inventory is readable on-chain and is dominated by HBTC, the Huobi-wrapped bitcoin, with BTCB, XRPB, KAVA, BNB, and a sliver of stablecoins behind it, and the collateral value still exceeds outstanding supply. That is why backing is the strongest of the three pillars even as the {{grade}} overall grade sits at the floor: {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} has not been enough to defend the peg, no viable exit path is established, and the active depeg caps the card by design. Mint caps and parameters are raiseable by a small stability committee and by KAVA stake governance, and the chain's governance can pause sends of the usdx denom, though it has not done so. Its tracking value is mostly analytical: it shows how a fully collateralized debt token can still trade far from par when nothing forces convergence.

xtusd-xt.title: XT.com XSC CDP Dollar
xtusd-xt.text: XTUSD is XT.com's exchange-issued dollar, and its live deployment on XSC is a Maker-style Vat carrying one debt-bearing collateral type: roughly 4.3 million XTUSD borrowed against Wrapped XT.
