What the on-chain read found is what is missing. No Spotter, price feed, or other update contract is authorized on that Vat. The collateral price sits at a fixed value with no identified mechanism to move it. No Cat, Dog, auction, or global-settlement module is authorized either. The 2022 announcement that promised a 150% minimum collateral ratio and an auction for risky vaults is half true: the 3% annual fee matches the Jug's duty exactly, so the interest accrues as advertised, while the auction it is supposed to protect has no contract standing behind it. The Median/OSM/Spotter stack that does exist on XSC is wired to the issuer's legacy TAI deployment, not to this one. Pharos caps the card on that finding: an opaque collateral-price path is a critical oracle signal, and it binds the {{grade}} overall grade, because an unpriced, unliquidatable vault lacks the machinery a higher grade would measure.

hbd-hive.title: The Hive Conversion Dollar
hbd-hive.text: HBD is Hive's {{term:algorithmic}}algorithmic{{/term}} dollar, a protocol-native claim redeemable on-chain for $1 of HIVE through a witness-median conversion, with haircut rules when system debt exceeds thresholds. It targets $1 through HIVE conversion rules and witness-set savings parameters, not through cash or Treasury {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. That makes the collateral base reflexive to the value and governance of Hive itself, especially under haircut conditions. Pharos classifies HBD as crypto-backed and decentralized while flagging that the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop is protocol conversion capacity, not liquid off-chain reserves. The market priced that distinction in earnest in late July 2026, when HBD slid roughly a tenth below the dollar on sparse venues before clawing back to within a few percent of the peg. At the late-August review the consensus debt ratio stood above the 20% print-stop threshold and below the 30% haircut line, so new HBD issuance was paused while conversions still paid full value. The defense mechanism is conversion into the very asset holders are fleeing, which is why the exit pillar is the weakest line on the {{grade}} report card.

jpyc-jpyc-v1.title: The Legacy JPYC Series
jpyc-jpyc-v1.text: Legacy prepaid-payment yen token series predating JPYC's funds-transfer-token migration; retained only for discovery and validation. JPY Coin v1 is the older JPYC token series, separate from the current JPYC deployment already tracked by Pharos. It is backed by yen-denominated reserve obligations and legacy redemption processes rather than the newer funds-transfer-token contracts. The Ethereum, Polygon, and Gnosis deployments are retained for discovery and reserve validation. Its main reason to track separately is migration clarity, because the old and current JPYC contracts are not interchangeable. The legacy prepaid {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} model and its narrower {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} processes are the reason v1 is not interchangeable with the current FSA-licensed JPYC contract.

nxusd-nereus.title: The Nereus CDP Dollar
nxusd-nereus.text: NXUSD is a crypto-backed debt token minted through Nereus Finance on Avalanche and Polygon via {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} mechanics, and the market around it has gone quiet: Pharos carries the price feed at low confidence, and the token has drifted on both sides of par, including a brief discount of several hundred basis points in July 2026. The peg line on the card still reads well because those episodes were short, which is why Pharos pairs the {{grade}} overall grade with an exit pillar that is the weakest of the three rather than taking the quiet tape at face value. No same-notional redemption route is disclosed, and the primary exit is undisclosed. The reserve stack is modeled as {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} lending positions across seventeen Avalanche cauldrons, but Nereus publishes no per-market collateral weights, which leaves the notional backing dependent on collateral volatility, {{term:liquidation}}liquidations{{/term}}, and single-source oracle routes, none of it verified by a liquid par {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path. NXUSD fits the dormant CDP relic pattern: transparent enough to track, illiquid enough that the tracking mostly documents stillness.

wemix-dollar-wemix.title: The WEMIX Ecosystem Dollar
wemix-dollar-wemix.text: WEMIX Dollar has completed the arc its replacement plan wrote for it: the Foundation moved the ecosystem's dollar activity to bridged USDC.e, withdrew its liquidity from WEMIX$ pools, and ended swap support across WEMIX.Fi and WEMIX PLAY in April 2026, and Pharos formally froze the listing on 2026-07-11 as a confirmed wind-down. What remains is an orderly wind-down rather than a collapse. Holders kept a conversion route through the WEMIX$ Module and a longer claim window for discontinued pools, which is more exit courtesy than most retired stablecoins ever extend. The design was always an issuer-managed ecosystem unit. It had USDC backing in the WEMIX3.0 Treasury with DIOS stabilization on a chain Pharos never indexed, so outside validation of the reserves was never possible, and now it never will be. Its epitaph doubles as the genre's lesson: a game-chain dollar that never escaped its home chain proved easier to replace with another issuer's dollar than to keep running.

suiusde-sui.title: Sui Ethena-Style Synthetic Dollar
suiusde-sui.text: suiUSDe is Sui's Ethena-whitelabel synthetic dollar. The token keeps USDe's design while adding a new chain label. Ethena's whitelabel transparency feed identifies the backing as predominantly USDe with a smaller USDC sleeve, held across Anchorage and Coinbase custody wallets and a Sui mint-redeem wallet, so the reserve inherits USDe's {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}} hedging, {{term:basis-trade}}basis-trade{{/term}} execution, off-exchange {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, and exchange dependency. The Sui-specific twist is deployment control: a single admin role holder also controls the package upgrade path, so chain-native does not mean governance-light. The peg record is the strongest line on the card. Exit is the weakest pillar, because minting and redemption run through USDC only, priced by a single Pyth feed and gated by eligibility, with no comparable secondary route reviewed. The {{grade}} overall grade reflects that split: verified backing above a thin, permissioned exit.

vcred-vcred.title: The Hemi Credit Dollar
vcred-vcred.text: vCRED is a Hemi-based credit-token dollar with thin public reserve detail: the product site publishes an estimated APY and aggregate volume but no NAV, pricing methodology, valuation cadence, reserve composition, or {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, so Pharos carries the backing as one undisclosed envelope of protocol credit and crypto collateral rather than a verified reserve. The tracked token itself is a plain owner-mintable, holder-burnable ERC-20 with no oracle, {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}, or exchange-rate input, and mint() answers to a 1-of-2 Safe, which is why economic control is the weakest pillar on a card where all three sit at the floor. There is no freeze or blacklist function in the bytecode, so transfers are permissionless, but that is the only permissionless thing about it: no comparable exit route is supported and redemption depth is undisclosed. The result is a tracked but high-risk long-tail dollar where the collateral, the valuation, and the way out all remain operationally opaque.

mai-qidao.title: Debt That Cannot Be Liquidated
mai-qidao.text: MAI is a multi-collateral {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} dollar whose most important number is the share of its loan book that no longer functions. An on-chain sweep of 71 QiDao vault contracts across twelve chains found roughly 2.1 million MAI of recorded vault debt, and about 72% of it sits in fifteen Fantom markets where every price source reverts. Because the price call fails, {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}}, collateral withdrawal, and new borrowing all revert with it: this is Multichain-era debt that cannot be cleared, only waited out, and QiDao's own site describes the Fantom position as a dispute whose tokens return to holders once resolved. The markets that do still price read exactly one Chainlink feed with no staleness check, no heartbeat enforcement, and no fallback, and no deployment carries a stability pool or insurance fund. The stabilityPool address is zero everywhere it was probed. Even on live chains some vaults are too far underwater to liquidate at all, because the collateral payout underflows before the keeper can be paid. The {{grade}} grade is an accounting of what is left standing.

spusd-soulpeg.title: The SoulPeg Dollar
spusd-soulpeg.text: spUSD is SoulPeg's freely tradable BNB Chain wrapper around a soul-bound sUSDC position, with every deposited USDC routed through Venus lending markets. Pharos tracks the reserve as a single USDC dependency deployed into Venus, so the backing question is Circle plus lending-market liquidity rather than an undisclosed basket. The gap is on the exit side: Pharos has not source-reviewed a holder-exercisable USDC {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} route for spUSD, so no redemption backstop is modeled and exit is the weakest of the three pillars. A single admin key can also authorize arbitrary holder burns on the token. Until a reviewable redemption route and custody terms appear, spUSD remains a small protocol-dependent dollar rather than a high-confidence stablecoin, and its {{grade}} overall grade reflects that.

inalpha-nest.title: The Nest Vault Share
inalpha-nest.text: inALPHA is Nest Credit's NAV-priced dollar vault token, holding private and structured credit positions with nTBILL and liquid stablecoin buffers; providers classify it as dollar-referenced, but it behaves like a vault share rather than a par stablecoin. The token can appreciate or drift with vault strategy performance, so Pharos marks it {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} and NAV-style. Reserve validation reads the Nest positions API, but no fixed reserve composition has been reviewed, so the {{grade}} report card scores the backing as undisclosed and the exit pillar as its weakest line because primary {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} is eligibility-gated through the authorized Teller under a 3-of-6 Safe. The vault also shares its redemption rail with the other Nest products Pharos tracks, a concentration the card records. This is useful coverage, but direct comparisons with cash-backed dollars are misleading. The underlying mix is {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} credit with an nTBILL {{term:treasury}}T-bill{{/term}} buffer, so redemption depth depends on the vault's liquid stablecoin layer rather than direct par exit.

eusd-telcoin.title: The Telcoin Bank Dollar
eusd-telcoin.text: Telcoin eUSD is a bank-issued dollar token from Telcoin Digital Asset Bank, operating under Nebraska's digital-asset depository framework rather than the usual offshore issuer maze. That regulatory posture is stronger than most long-tail additions, but Pharos still keeps the reserve slice conservative because detailed public telemetry and published monthly attestations are not yet as mature as the charter story: the customer agreement defines the permitted reserve envelope of insured deposits, Treasuries and agency paper, but names no reserve bank and publishes no weights, which leaves backing the weakest pillar on a card graded {{grade}} overall. The token spans Ethereum, Base, Polygon, and Solana, with issuer and multisig controls doing the minting work behind the scenes and a Solana freeze authority held by the issuer. Redemption is a KYC-gated banking-rail process, and that rail is what the exit pillar, the strongest of the three, is grading; the trust boundary is the bank. The charter started paying rent in June, when Telcoin launched the first U.S. regulated on-chain bank accounts tied natively to eUSD through its Wallet V5: deposit banking and a stablecoin sharing one regulated container. eUSD is what happens when a stablecoin gets a bank charter before it gets market depth, and the bank part is no longer theoretical.

money-defi-money.title: The defi.money Stablecoin
money-defi-money.text: MONEY is defi.money's crypto-backed loan stablecoin, closer to a crvUSD-style CDP than to a fixed reserve wrapper with tidy bank statements. Users deposit approved collateral such as WBTC and ETH, borrow against market-specific risk parameters, and rely on conversion ranges and liquidations to keep the system solvent. Pharos treats the reserve as protocol-approved crypto loan collateral and validates it through curated on-chain checks, but the live collateral mix is still less transparent than the larger CDP systems it echoes. The mint path is user-collateralized, while market onboarding and debt ceilings remain under partially bounded admin control. It is a serious fork of a serious design, which still leaves plenty of room for governance knobs to matter.

fusd-freedom-dollar.title: The Zano Privacy Dollar
fusd-freedom-dollar.text: FUSD is a Zano privacy-chain dollar token minted against staked ZANO reserves, with no Pharos-supported chain {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}} and no contract Pharos can attach, so reserve sync cannot run and the record rests on the issuer's own disclosures. Those disclosures are more than they were: the Freedom Dollar homepage publishes a live reserve widget showing the ZANO reserve wallet, the fUSD held back in reserve, and a coverage ratio above one at Pharos's early-September read, and the white paper describes a market-making design that targets one dollar's worth of ZANO. What the on-chain record adds is less comforting. Issuance is a consensus-level EMIT operation that a single asset-owner key can sign up to a ceiling far above circulation, and the white paper's DAO and over-collateralization language is an off-chain operating policy that Zano consensus never checks. The bots' ZANO/USD input, fallback, and shortfall procedure are unpublished, so the oracle path is reviewed as opaque. With no independent {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} or verifiable {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} disclosures, the {{grade}} overall grade is bounded by that opaque oracle topology and by an exit that only a ZANO-denominated market can provide.

fusd-finchain.title: A Rebasing Bermuda Dollar
fusd-finchain.text: FinChain Dollar is a BMA-licensed, {{term:yield-bearing}}rebasing{{/term}} dollar backed by tokenized U.S. Treasury bill and {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market fund{{/term}} products. The token targets a fixed $1 value while balances rebase daily, so the yield shows up as more FUSD instead of a rising NAV. FinChain's own reserve pages name Taikang, ChinaAMC, and BNY Mellon fund products, but they publish no per-product weights, the reserve dashboard shows only aggregate placeholders, and the issuer's data API was last updated in April 2026. That gap shows on the {{grade}} overall grade: backing and exit are the two weakest pillars, for undisclosed composition and eligibility-gated redemption, while the peg itself has tracked par since launch. The main caveats are issuer concentration, eligible-customer access, and reserve transparency that remains issuer-led with no independent reconciliation.

zsd-zephyr-protocol.title: The Zephyr Privacy Dollar
zsd-zephyr-protocol.text: Zephyr Stable Dollar is a Djed-inspired {{term:algorithmic}}algorithmic{{/term}} dollar on Zephyr's Monero-derived private chain, minted and redeemed against the protocol's native ZEPH reserve with reserve-ratio constraints intended to preserve {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}}. Pharos sources ZSD supply and the reserve ratio from Zephyr's own scanner API, since the chain is not a supported contract path, and keeps the reserve slice high risk because the backing asset is volatile native ZEPH. The reserve has recently reported several times the ZSD liability in ZEPH, which is why backing is the strongest of the three pillars. Economic control is the weakest line on the {{grade}} card: every node validates pricing records against a single hard-coded RSA key controlled by the Zephyr foundation and may reuse the last accepted price for up to ten blocks, so one signing authority sits under every mint, redemption, and reserve-ratio gate. There is no admin mint path and no holder freeze; the failure domain is chain consensus and its oracle input.

zys-zephyr-protocol.title: The Zephyr Yield Share
zys-zephyr-protocol.text: Zephyr Yield Share is the NAV-style {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} wrapper for Zephyr's ZSD yield reserve, tracked separately from base ZSD so that protocol yield is attributed to the token that actually earns it. ZYS supply, price, and APY come from Zephyr Scanner because CoinGecko and DefiLlama do not expose the wrapper as a market row. Each share is a consensus-level claim on the ZSD yield reserve, minted and redeemed through native MINT_YIELD and REDEEM_YIELD transactions with no admin mint route and no holder freeze. The {{grade}} overall grade is a ceiling rather than the wrapper's own arithmetic: a child cannot rate above the ZSD it requires, and ZYS inherits Zephyr's private-chain and {{term:algorithmic}}algorithmic{{/term}} ZEPH-collateral risk through that dependency. Economic control is the weakest pillar for the same reason as ZSD, a single hard-coded oracle signing key under the yield-reserve accrual, while the backing review covers only the ZSD layer and leaves the upstream reserve question open.

iusd-indigo-protocol.title: The Cardano Synthetic Dollar
iusd-indigo-protocol.text: iUSD is Indigo Protocol's synthetic dollar on Cardano, minted against overcollateralized {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} vaults of ADA and DAO-whitelisted native tokens, with governed peg-stability modules that can mint or redeem against approved stablecoins. Its risk profile is a classic crypto-CDP profile: collateral volatility against the {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} ratio, {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} execution through per-asset Stability Pools, oracle quality, and DAO governance all matter. Pharos now reads the composition from Indigo's public CDP index and Koios supply: at the September 2026 review roughly nine tenths of iUSD debt sat on ADA collateral, a sliver on NIGHT, and a residual of several percent could not be attributed to individual vaults or the USDCx peg module, so it is carried as unresolved rather than normalised away. The {{grade}} report card is weakest on exit, and economic control is held down by an oracle topology that relies on a single Pyth Lazer feed per branch with no documented fallback. The peg record has stayed clean for as long as Pharos has tracked it. The durable constraint is that iUSD is only as liquid and as well-priced as the Cardano venues and feeds beneath it.

cdp-enosys.title: Flare's CDP Experiment
cdp-enosys.text: CDP is Enosys Loans' Flare-native dollar, minted against FXRP, wFLR, sFLR, and stXRP vaults priced by the Flare Time Series Oracle. The mechanism is a Liquity V2 friendly fork: user-set borrow rates, a Stability Pool for liquidations, and redemptions against the lowest-rate positions when the market stops pretending one CDP is worth one dollar. That is a more interesting peg engine than another issuer IOU, and it shows on the {{grade}} card, where backing and exit are the two strong pillars and economic control is the weakest. The control finding is specific: the token proxy's 2-of-6 Safe owner can register arbitrary addresses as branch contracts, which grants forced-transfer and burn authority over holder balances, an EOA owns the proxy admin, and the oracle connector discards the FTSO timestamp and enforces no maximum age, so a stale price never triggers branch shutdown. FXRP, itself an agent-collateralized XRP representation, is most of the collateral, so Flare collateral depth is the other standing exposure. It is decentralized enough to be mechanically legible, and not decentralized enough to make admin risk disappear.

luausd-lumi-finance.title: The Lumi Floor-Dollar
luausd-lumi-finance.text: Lumi Finance LUAUSD is a dollar-referenced synthetic on Arbitrum tied to LUA floor-price and protocol-owned liquidity mechanics rather than 1:1 fiat {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}, so Pharos marks it as NAV-style and high risk. The Arbitrum contract enables curated validation, but the reserve slice is intentionally broad because public proof is weak: the split between LUA collateral and USDT/USDC protocol-owned liquidity is unpublished. Lumi's current documentation states that circulating LUAUSD can be exchanged for USDT 1:1, yet the token has traded persistently below $1, and the mint is an owner-only call behind a 3-of-5 Safe with no cap, so minting is scored as unbounded. With no comparable exit route compiled, the exit pillar is the weakest on the card. This entry is included for provider coverage, with a warning that the stability claim is nonstandard. The peg claim is closer to an {{term:algorithmic}}algorithmic{{/term}} floor-price reference than fiat backing, and no third-party {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} is modelled by Pharos.

susd-solayer.title: Solayer Token-2022 Treasury Dollar
susd-solayer.text: Solayer sUSD is a Solana Token-2022 interest-bearing dollar whose balances grow from Treasury-bill exposure instead of staying as a static par token. Since November 2025 the reserve instrument has been OpenEden's cUSDO, a tokenized Treasury product issued by OpenEden Digital with Adam Eve Capital managing the underlying bills, held through Solayer's qualified liquidity providers. Solayer workflows handle minting, the interest extension handles balance growth, and the mint, freeze, and rate authorities resolve to a Solayer program that a plain keypair can upgrade. Backing is the weakest of the three pillars: the reserve asset and obligor are identified, but the Treasury-fund mix, custodian split, and provider balances are not published, so the fixed-input composition remains incomplete and the evidence ceiling stays low. Exit depends on Solayer's issuer workflows and institutional custody assumptions. Peg history has been clean on the limited price coverage available, and the {{grade}} overall grade reflects identified but thinly evidenced backing behind a single-entity issuer. Whether a yield-passing token of this kind counts as a payment stablecoin under the GENIUS Act is unresolved.

usx-dforce.title: Overcollateralized on Paper
usx-dforce.text: dForce USD is now a read-only archive: Pharos froze USX on 2026-07-18 after it slid to roughly $0.39 with on-chain liquidity measured in tens of thousands of dollars and daily volume under $10. The {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-style design launched in 2021 and peaked above $205M in mid-2022, but it never truly recovered from that bear market. Legacy debt positions on the dForce/Unitus lending protocol left circulating USX without a credible par-{{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} route, and the discount widened from cents to a chasm over four years. The terminal slide was orderly in the way glaciers are: below $0.75 in February 2026, below $0.45 by April, and near $0.39 by the July freeze, with the DF governance token near zero and no published remediation plan to point at. The epitaph writes itself: {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} on paper, unredeemable in practice. Collateral you cannot claim at par is balance-sheet decoration, not a backstop.

home-homecoin.title: The Property-Lien Dollar
home-homecoin.text: HOME is HomeCoin's dollar stablecoin backed by U.S. home-loan liens and property-backed receivables originated through Bacon Protocol, rather than cash, T-bills, or crypto collateral. That makes the asset interesting but illiquid: HOME mints and redeems 1:1 for USDC through Bacon's Pan contract only as far as Pan liquidity allows, and beyond that the fallback is a foreclosure right, which is not the same thing as {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} liquidity. Reserve risk is dominated by mortgage-lien {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} quality rather than cash {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}: the issuer publishes no current loan tape, valuation cadence, or independent report, so Pharos scores the entire collateral category as undisclosed. Pharos marks HOME yield-bearing on the basis of home-loan payment distributions. The {{grade}} overall grade is held down on two fronts. The exit pillar is the weakest line because no comparable same-notional route is documented, and economic control is nearly as weak because the token sits behind a proxy whose 3-of-5 legacy multisig can upgrade it with no timelock. The peg has held close to par on the single thin venue that trades it. The durable constraint is that a lien portfolio cannot be turned into dollars on demand.

cdxusd-cod3x.title: The Facilitator-Minted Dollar
cdxusd-cod3x.text: cdxUSD is Cod3x's dollar stablecoin on Base, minted and burned by protocol-permissioned Facilitators within assigned bucket limits against strategy-managed crypto and stablecoin collateral, a GHO-style model that concentrates risk in facilitator permissions, collateral management, and strategy transparency. The live token exposes exactly one Facilitator, a 3-of-9 Safe labeled Multisig with a 100 million cdxUSD bucket, and the whitepaper's lending-liquidation and AMO facilitators are not deployed; the token owner is a 24-hour timelock. No current source publishes the facilitator collateral inventory or coverage ratio, so Pharos carries a single high-risk reserve slice with no composition, and the ABI exposes no holder-callable burn-for-reserve {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}: a Facilitator burn is not a holder exit. On the {{grade}} card backing and exit both sit at the bottom of the scale for those reasons, and the oracle finding is opaque because the Safe values its own collateral under rules the protocol does not publish. Facilitator-managed minting resembles a permissioned {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} variant rather than a public {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}}; the peg has held on the tracked feed, but with no disclosed reserves that record is price, not proof.

susd-hedgecore.title: HedgeCore Venus Yield Wrapper
susd-hedgecore.text: HedgeCore sUSD is a BSC yield wrapper minted from USDC and routed through Venus lending. The reserve dependency is explicit: USDC enters HedgeCore's strategy layer, earns through Venus, and gets reflected back through operator-mediated reward and exit mechanics. HedgeCore's documentation describes the token as soul-bound, but the verified contract executes ordinary transfers except where a wrapper lock is active, and the wrapper owner can burn a named holder's balance without allowance. Pharos marks it yield-bearing but keeps the APY source conservative because a reliable public pool feed is not part of the current data path. Exit is the weakest pillar: early redemption is operator-controlled, the hUSDC wrapper only opens one direction, and no comparable redemption route is disclosed. The {{grade}} overall grade reflects a clean peg record sitting on an undisclosed exit and a single-entity admin.

usd3-reserve-protocol.title: The Reserve Basket Dollar
usd3-reserve-protocol.text: USD3 is a Reserve Protocol RToken/DTF that turns yield-bearing wrappers into a dollar basket, which is clever until you count the upstream assumptions. The backing is split across Savings USDS, Aave USDC, wrapped Compound USDCv3, and Steakhouse USDC strategy exposure, so holders are buying a governed portfolio of stablecoin yield rather than a single clean reserve. Reserve's real-time protocol feed and basket redemption mechanics make the structure more inspectable than most wrapper stacks. RSR stakers and governance absorb and manage losses, but that also means parameter choices and collateral onboarding matter as much as the assets themselves. USD3 is a tidy DeFi balance-sheet product whose {{grade}} overall grade is bounded by the basket rather than the wrapper: backing is the weakest of the three pillars because the token can be no safer than the stablecoin yield positions it holds.

sofid-sofi.title: The Fed's Own Stablecoin Customer
sofid-sofi.text: SoFiUSD is what happens when a nationally chartered U.S. bank decides the stablecoin wrapper is worth adding to old-fashioned cash at the Federal Reserve. Reserves sit at SoFi Bank's Fed master account, with BitGo running 1:1 mint and redemption on an upgradeable, bank-controlled contract. The distribution question got its answer in May 2026, when SoFi opened the token to its nearly 15 million app members, making SOFID the first national-bank stablecoin offered directly inside a consumer banking app. What has not arrived is a number: no permitted market-data source reports a positive circulating supply or market cap, so Pharos has temporarily withheld the listing until the figures exist. The attestation story is similarly aspirational. Press coverage mentions monthly Deloitte verification, but no public attestation report or transparency page has materialized. A bank that can put a stablecoin in front of fifteen million customers but not a supply figure in front of anyone is running bank-grade issuance with bank-grade opacity, and only one of those is a compliment.

sources.label: SoFi press release: SoFiUSD retail launch to nearly 15M members (May 27, 2026)

usdb-bridge.title: Stripe Bridge USDB Payments Rail
usdb-bridge.text: Bridge's USDB is Stripe's stablecoin rail, with reserves in cash and BlackRock {{term:money-market-fund}}MMFs{{/term}} under a conditional OCC trust charter and distribution embedded in Stripe's payment flow, so most people who touch it will never know they are using it. Bridge, Stripe's stablecoin subsidiary, powers Stablecoin Financial Accounts in 101 countries, turning every Stripe merchant into a potential stablecoin endpoint without the merchant ever touching a token. The OCC conditional national trust bank charter from February 2026 gives Bridge the federal regulatory cover that most stablecoin issuers spend years pursuing, with institutional {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} behind the reserves. Stripe can embed stablecoin settlement into existing payment flows without asking permission from anyone downstream, and Bridge Open Issuance now also mints branded dollars for MoneyGram and Deel. Pharos holds USDB at pre-launch until a verified runtime price and circulating-supply source exists; the DefiLlama rows carrying the USDB ticker today belong to Blast USDB and FantOHM.

sources.label: Ledger Insights: Stripe rolls out stablecoin accounts in 101 countries as Bridge launches USDB
CoinDesk: Bridge wins initial approval of national trust bank charter

hkdap-anchorpoint.title: The Proof Nobody Checks
hkdap-anchorpoint.text: The first HKMA-licensed HKD stablecoin under the Stablecoins Ordinance, now live in an institution-only beta and finally measurable. After two missed launch windows, HKDAP went out on August 12 2026 attested by its distributors rather than its issuer. OSL Group and HashKey Exchange announced themselves as authorised, while anchorpoint.hk read "has not yet officially launched." DefiLlama picked the token up on August 27, and the Ethereum deployment's supply, a few hundred thousand HKDAP in its first weeks, is now independently verifiable. On August 14 BlockSec published a review of that same contract: the KYC proof argument is passed in and then discarded, so any proof, including an empty string, passes; de-registering a compromised KYC provider does not stop the wallets it onboarded from transacting; a single key can mint, burn, pause, or freeze, with two keys controlling every upgrade and role and no timelocks or multi-signature anywhere on the high-risk path. Debug logging left in the proxy fallback, an optimizer set to zero runs, and test files uploaded to Etherscan point to a pre-production build sitting on mainnet. The regulator vetted the issuer, not the bytecode. Pharos still holds HKDAP pre-launch, though the reason has changed: supply is no longer missing; price is, with DefiLlama reporting null and CoinGecko carrying a preview listing with no market data. The licensing playbook rests on segregated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, HKMA-mandated {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, and a regulated {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path scoped for HKD-denominated {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} settlement. None of this is enforced by the contract that actually moves the tokens.

hkd-hsbc.title: PayMe Gets a Blockchain
hkd-hsbc.text: HSBC's HKD stablecoin is the second HKMA-licensed entry, pre-launch with an H2 2026 target, and the one with the distribution advantage that matters: 3.3 million PayMe users who already use the app for peer-to-peer payments and won't need to download anything new. The integration into HSBC's HK App for tokenized investment subscriptions points to the actual product thesis. HSBC is building a settlement layer for its own digital asset products, with standalone DeFi as a secondary use case. The reserves will be HKD-denominated high-quality liquid assets in segregated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} accounts per HKMA rules with HKMA-mandated {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} routed through PayMe and the HSBC HK app, and the symbol hasn't even been confirmed yet. The interesting tension: HSBC is building a stablecoin specifically to avoid depending on anyone else's stablecoin, which is either strategic autonomy or institutional NIH syndrome depending on your perspective.

okrw-hashed.title: Korea Builds Its Own Chain
okrw-hashed.text: OKRW is the pre-launch native KRW stablecoin of Maroo, the Layer 1 that Hashed Open Finance built specifically to host it. Maroo is positioned as the first 'sovereign L1' purpose-built for Korean Won stablecoins, with a dual-track design that offers both a regulated path (bank-backed, KYC-gated) and an open path (permissionless issuance). The testnet went live in May 2026 with OKRW as the native token, and mainnet is targeted before year-end. In a country where crypto trading volumes regularly rival the stock market but regulated stablecoin infrastructure is virtually nonexistent, the thesis is less about technology and more about regulatory positioning: whoever builds the compliant KRW on-ramp first captures a market that has been using USDT as a proxy currency by default.

arc-anq.title: The Rupee's On-Chain Debut
arc-anq.text: ARC is India's first attempt at a regulated rupee stablecoin, built by Anq with Polygon's backing and designed for a 1:1 INR peg backed by cash, fixed deposits, and Indian government securities. Its stated purpose is to stem the USD liquidity outflow that India's regulators have been panicking about since USDT volumes on Indian exchanges started dwarfing domestic payment rail throughput. It reads like a mutual fund prospectus, with {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} at regulated Indian banks, and the two-tier framework is explicitly designed to complement rather than compete with the RBI's digital rupee CBDC. The Uniswap v4 whitelisting for compliance is a novel technical approach to the 'permissioned token on a permissionless chain' problem, and primary {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} will run through KYC-gated issuer rails rather than open market making. The tentative January 2026 debut passed with no RBI confirmation and no live supply, and in July 2026 the RBI told a Parliamentary Standing Committee it favours barring banks and regulated entities from private stablecoins, rupee-backed ones included. Whether India's regulatory apparatus will actually let a private rupee stablecoin operate alongside its CBDC remains the existential question that no amount of technical architecture can answer.

sources.label: CoinDesk: India's debt-backed ARC token eyes tentative January 2026 debut
Payment Expert: RBI signals preference to bar regulated entities from private stablecoins (2026-07-08)

brl-b3.title: The Stock Exchange Mints Money
brl-b3.text: BRL-B3 is a pre-launch Brazilian real settlement stablecoin from B3, Latin America's largest stock exchange, designed for its tokenized {{term:rwa}}real-world-asset{{/term}} trading platform. When Latin America's largest stock exchange decides it needs its own stablecoin for tokenized asset settlement, the signal is less about crypto adoption and more about what traditional financial infrastructure considers table stakes in 2026. B3's BRL stablecoin is branded B3RL, built on Polygon, and backed by cash and government bonds inside B3's own clearing infrastructure. It fills the gap left by Brazil's Drex CBDC narrowing its scope: the central bank's digital currency was meant to handle settlement, but as that project slowed, B3 decided to build the settlement rails itself. The timeline has moved: the first-half-of-2026 window floated at May's Tokenization Day has come and gone, and by July's Expert XP conference the line had softened to a launch 'in the coming months,' with asset tokenization itself pushed to early 2027. B3 clears trillions annually. The open questions are whether Brazil's regulators will let a stock exchange run the settlement rails the central bank once reserved for itself and whether 'coming months' survives contact with the CVM.

usdf-flipcash.title: Coinbase's White-Label Dollar
usdf-flipcash.text: Flipcash's USDF is the first stablecoin minted through Coinbase's Custom Stablecoins platform, a stablecoin-as-a-service product that lets any business launch a branded dollar backed 1:1 by USDC. Flipcash is the test case, and the product itself is less interesting than the platform it proves out: if Custom Stablecoins works, every fintech, neobank, and loyalty program can have its own branded dollar without touching reserve management. The dependency chain is explicit: USDF is a wrapper around USDC, so its backing is only as good as Circle's reserve stack. Governance is centralized-dependent because the token's existence depends on Coinbase continuing to operate the platform. USDF went live on Solana in May 2026 with Coinbase Onramp fiat access, but as of July 2026 it remained in Coinbase-exchange operational-only backend testing with no trading, deposits, or withdrawals, no public Solana mint address, and no DefiLlama or CoinGecko listing under the Flipcash identity, so it cannot yet enter Pharos runtime data. Whether the market needs branded USDC wrappers or whether this is a new distribution channel for Circle's existing product stays open; until a public supply surface exists, USDF is a platform demonstration.

sources.label: Crypto Briefing: Coinbase debuts Custom Stablecoins, USDF by Flipcash launches as first partner
Yahoo Finance: Coinbase experiments, Flipcash USDF rolls out as first Custom Stablecoin

krw-imbank.title: Quantum-Resistant Won
krw-imbank.text: iM Bank's KRW stablecoin proof-of-concept on Kaia is symbolic of a regulatory thaw rather than a commercial product, and it has a feature that most stablecoins won't need for a decade but makes excellent press releases: quantum-resistant post-quantum cryptography via BTQ Technologies. Set aside the security theater angle, and the actual significance is that a Korean commercial bank is building a KRW stablecoin at all. South Korea's regulatory stance on private stablecoins has been cautious to the point of paralysis, and a bank-led PoC signals that the regulatory ice may be thawing. The Finger partnership handles the wallet and DeFi integration layer, while iM Bank brings the banking license and the KRW reserves. Whether this moves beyond proof-of-concept depends entirely on whether Korean regulators want to compete with Hashed's OKRW for the title of first regulated KRW stablecoin or whether they'd prefer neither existed. As a bank-issued PoC, the stack assumes regulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} of KRW reserves, statutory {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, and a banking-rail {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path that has yet to face commercial traffic.

gldy-streamex.title: The Yield-Bearing Gold Ounce
gldy-streamex.text: GLDY is Streamex's {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} tokenized gold ounce on Base: each token represents one troy ounce of bullion, with gold-leasing receivables through Monetary Metals as the source of returns paid in additional gold. Reserve evidence is stronger than most new commodity tokens carry. An EisnerAmper examination as of March 2026 reported reserve ounces at or above tokens outstanding, and a Chainlink feed on Base publishes the issuer-reported ounce count daily, although that feed transports Streamex's own figures rather than attesting them independently. The main caveat is that the yield comes from issuer-managed gold leasing rather than passive vault storage, so lease-counterparty concentration and bar-level custody allocation remain undisclosed. The exit pillar is the weakest line on the {{grade}} report card: primary-market {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} is limited to eligible investors and the route carries no explicit same-notional USD output, so Pharos records the primary exit as undisclosed. Control sits with Streamex: two admin paths, one of them a single key, can grant minters, change the reserve-oracle configuration, or upgrade the contract without a timelock. GLDY is tracked as a commodity token issued as a restricted security for accredited investors, and that eligibility gate is the durable constraint on the claim.

sources.label: Streamex press release: first independent reserve attestation (2026-07-01)

vnxau-vnx.title: The Liechtenstein Gram-Gold Token
vnxau-vnx.text: VNX Gold represents one gram of physical gold and fits the same Liechtenstein regulated-issuer pattern as VNX's fiat tokens. AREVA's agreed-upon-procedures report as of 31 December 2025 reconciled 13,100 tokens across chains to 13,100 gross grams on Philoro Edelmetallhandel AG's custody statement, held in VNX Commodities AG's name, without physically observing the gold or validating quality, value, or legal title; {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}-style VNX documentation and an Ethereum supply probe provide lightweight live sync until a stronger public reserve API is available. Redemption is meaningful but operationally constrained: verified platform users can sell or request physical delivery from one-kilogram bar denominations, and no score-eligible runtime route exists, so exit is the weakest pillar on the card while economic control is the strongest. The risk is less the gold unit and more the issuer, custody, and platform access path.

sources.label: AREVA VNXAU agreed-upon procedures report as of December 31, 2025

xagm-matrixdock.title: Matrixdock's Silver Ounce
xagm-matrixdock.text: Matrixdock's silver token entered the Bureau Veritas programme this year. XAGm's first inclusion involved a full physical count of 66 Good Delivery bars against the parcel ownership list, with no anomalies. The certificate examines the vault as of the end of June, and Pharos dates composition to when the work was done rather than when the PDF was posted, so the audited composition already sits outside the v9 freshness bound and the card carries a staleness cap until the next cycle. The count also exposes the deeper gap: XAGm tokens appear nowhere in the certificate. This is assets-only physical inventory: an inspection of metal with no reconciliation to what has been issued against it. It is paired with a mint path the authority review reads as unbounded, since an operator can add local mint budget manually with only a four-hour request-to-execute delay in the way. Today the exit pillar is the weakest on the card: physical {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} is documented, but Pharos has compiled no score-eligible runtime route, and that gap holds the {{grade}} overall grade down. The bars are real; the arithmetic connecting them to your token remains entirely the issuer's to assert.

sources.label: Matrixdock Gold Bureau Veritas Audit Jul 2026 (covers XAUm gold and XAGm silver)
Matrixdock press release - two years of independent verification (2026-07-21)

gramg-token-teknoloji.title: Turkey's Gram-Gold Token
gramg-token-teknoloji.text: GRAMG is Token Teknoloji's one-gram gold claim from Turkey, and the open question is what, exactly, sits behind it: the issuer's product copy says equivalent PAXG is held on-chain, while the same page's FAQ and reserve disclosures describe physical gold at Turkish banks, the Central Bank, and company vaults. No current primary evidence reconciles the two stories. The reserve proof page does not help its own case: the supply widget renders empty, the evidence link points at an Ethereum address while the copy talks about Avalanche, and there is no independent {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, only the issuer's word at self-reported tier. {{term:redemption}}Redemption{{/term}} remains unscored because no reviewed direct-holder schedule has ever been published. Since mid-July 2026 the coin has been quarantined on Pharos because no permitted runtime source reports a positive circulating supply or market cap. It is a gold token whose backing form is disputed and whose token count is unverifiable. A gram of something is presumably somewhere; the disclosures cannot agree on what, and the data cannot confirm how much.

grams-token-teknoloji.title: Turkey's Gram-Silver Token
grams-token-teknoloji.text: GRAMS is Token Teknoloji's one-gram silver claim, the sibling of its gold product, with proof pages naming physical silver at Kuveyt Türk, VakıfBank, Ziraat Participation, and Akbank. The disclosure is at least consistently inconsistent: the product page describes company-vault {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} while the shared proof-of-reserves page names the banks, the reserve page reuses the gold token's contract address, and leftover platinum copy suggests the whole thing was assembled by find-and-replace. There is no independent {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}. The live feed Pharos wires up reads token supply on Avalanche, which proves the token exists, not that the silver does. {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} stays unmodeled because no direct-holder terms are documented. Since mid-July 2026 the coin has been quarantined on Pharos: no permitted runtime source reports a positive circulating supply or market cap. Somewhere in a Turkish vault there may be silver by the gram; the evidence trail stops several steps short of it.

euroe-membrane.title: Redemption-Only EUROe
euroe-membrane.text: EUROe is now best read in the past tense, which is not where a growth stablecoin wants to live. Membrane's Finnish EMI-licensed euro token has moved into Paxos' redemption-only wind-down after the product line was decommissioned, leaving holders with a 1:1 EUR exit path rather than an expanding on-chain euro network. The old reserve story was straightforward euro fiat and euro-denominated assets, but the current proof source is a redemption notice, not an ongoing reserve machine. Pharos still records the multichain contracts and regulated-entity posture, while the mint authority history shows EOA admin control and no heroic decentralization epilogue. EUROe's lesson is blunt: regulatory seriousness can make wind-down orderly, but it cannot make a discontinued token relevant.

gbpm-mento.title: Mento's CDP Pound
gbpm-mento.text: GBPm is Mento's British pound stablecoin on Celo, minted from {{term:cdp}}CDPs{{/term}} collateralized by USDm with oracle-priced {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}, extending Mento's Celo FX set into sterling on a Liquity v2 fork instead of the older shared reserve basket alone. Backing is therefore one tracked stablecoin exposure, USDm, which in turn rests on the shared Mento Reserve, and the public reserve API is a portfolio view, short of a full borrower-position inventory. The {{grade}} overall grade is led by the exit pillar, with Liquity-style redemption and Stability Pool liquidations giving holders a permissionless route out, while economic control is the weakest of the three: a 4-of-6 Mento Safe owns the token and can replace mint logic, and the TroveManager and Stability Pool hold burner and operator roles over any holder balance. The primary risk is dependency on Mento oracles, Celo execution, and USDm collateral quality.

jpym-mento.title: Mento's CDP Yen
jpym-mento.text: JPYm is a small but active yen stablecoin on Celo, backed by USDm collateral in Mento CDP troves, with the Mento reserve API exposing live CDP collateral. Supply and price now flow through DefiLlama, and the Mento API keeps reserve visibility aligned with GBPm and CHFm. Economic control is the weakest pillar on the card: a 4-of-6 Mento Safe can authorize minters and replace the Celo token implementation without delay. JPYm is tracked for strategic non-USD coverage, with liquidity and oracle dependency as the main caveats. As a Mento FX stablecoin, JPYm rests on a {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} with USDm {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} and oracle-priced FPMM swaps acting as the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} surface against the reserve.

chfm-mento.title: Mento's CDP Franc
chfm-mento.text: CHFm is Mento's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-backed Swiss franc stablecoin on Celo, minted by borrowers against USDm collateral rather than fiat reserves, which gives it a very different risk profile from fiat-backed VCHF or Frankencoin. The collateral rows are exposed directly by the Mento reserve API, so the backing path is visible enough for reserve tracking even though the asset is small. {{term:overcollateralization}}Overcollateralization{{/term}} at a 110% minimum ratio and {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} through the Stability Pool drive peg maintenance, and the exit pillar leads the card. The {{grade}} overall grade comes from the economic-control pillar, the weakest of the three: the token owner and proxy admin resolve to one 4-of-6 Mento Safe that can authorise a burner able to destroy any holder balance and can replace the implementation without delay. The residual risks are the single SortedOracles CHF/USD feed with no fallback, the USDm collateral path, and thin secondary liquidity.

bfusd-binance.title: Binance's Account Dollar
bfusd-binance.text: BFUSD is a Binance account product redeemable inside Binance against USD stablecoins, backed by a {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-hedged{{/term}} collateral pool, staked crypto, and a reserve fund, all legally and beneficially owned by Binance, leaving holders with product terms rather than claims. It was originally tracked for its CoinGecko coverage and large Binance user footprint, but {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} runs entirely through Binance-controlled terms that permit fees, limits, delays, and outright suspension, with self-reported, ad-hoc disclosures standing in for independent proof of reserves. Pharos delisted the entry in July 2026 as out of scope: BFUSD is a non-withdrawable account balance rather than a transferable production token, so there is no on-chain supply to measure and no independent {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} to verify. The strategy behind it may well be run competently: the point is that nobody outside Binance can check. A dollar you cannot withdraw, transfer, or audit is less a stablecoin than a database row with an APR.

pathusd-bridge.title: Tempo's Bridge Dollar
pathusd-bridge.text: pathUSD is the Bridge-issued dollar quote token for Tempo: users mint it by depositing USDC through Bridge-supported flows and redeem it back through Bridge {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} rails, against a reserve that Bridge describes as cash, short-dated Treasuries, overnight Treasury repo, and money-market-fund exposure with BlackRock and Fidelity as custody partners. The asset matters less for its current scale than for being native to a payment-focused chain that may become an important stablecoin rail. The {{grade}} overall grade is low, and the backing pillar is the weakest of the three: Bridge publishes no pathUSD-specific reserve report or allocation, the FAQ's quarterly audit statement is forward-looking only, and Pharos has no independent live reserve adapter for the portfolio, so the composition is scored as an unresolved basket. Redemption is eligibility-gated through Bridge, the TIP-20 token carries pause and blocked-account burn roles, and the issuance proxy's single admin can change both mint logic and the supply cap. The token launched in March 2026, so a short track record keeps the ceiling low until the reserve telemetry and the chain itself have history.

djed-coti.title: Cardano's Reserve-Coin Stable
djed-coti.text: DJED is Cardano's formally verified reserve-coin stablecoin: ADA sits in the reserve, DJED is the dollar claim, and SHEN absorbs surplus and volatility inside the protocol's 400% to 800% reserve-ratio band. That design gives the peg a clear mechanical buffer, and the reserve balance is readable at a single Cardano script address, but it also ties the whole system to ADA collateral risk and to the COTI/IOG oracle role. The minting policy is immutable Plutus code rather than a discretionary issuer desk, which is a real structural virtue, and there is no holder blacklist or freeze path. The {{grade}} overall grade is held back by the exit pillar, the weakest of the three: redemption is permissionless but runs only through the protocol's ADA reserve at a single aggregated ADA/USD rate, with no fiat route and thinner evidence behind it. DJED is one of the cleaner algorithmic-adjacent designs; the open question for every reserve-coin design is what happens when the reserve asset has a bad month.

usdv-solomon.title: The Ceffu Strategy Dollar
usdv-solomon.text: Solomon's USDv is a Solana synthetic dollar backed by Ceffu-custodied spot crypto hedged with Binance inverse perpetuals, a {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}} {{term:basis-trade}}basis trade{{/term}} run by Solomon Labs. The token supply is easy to validate on-chain, and Solomon now publishes a protocol-data API, but that feed is the problem rather than the answer: its identified reserve components cover under a third of reported protocol TVL, the remainder has no issuer-explained allocation, and the only external artefact is an aggregate, custodian-issued Ceffu attestation dated April 2026. Backing is therefore graded on a mostly unmapped book. Direct mint and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} are restricted to Solomon-approved participants against a small documented reserve buffer, with no permissionless holder rail, which makes exit the weakest of the three pillars on the {{grade}} card. Mint logic can be replaced by a 3-of-9 multisig with no timelock, and reconciliation of supply to reserves is unverified. The SPL mint's freeze authority is disabled, so holders cannot be frozen on-chain, but that is the one control Solomon has given up. USDv is a visible Solana dollar whose backing cannot be audited from the outside, and the card prices that gap.

fxd-fathom.title: XDC's Native CDP Dollar
fxd-fathom.text: FXD is Fathom's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-minted dollar on XDC, giving the XDC ecosystem a native {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} dollar backed by XDC and Fathom collateral-pool positions and stabilized by {{term:liquidation}}liquidations{{/term}} plus a stability module. Pharos's on-chain read shows the collateral is now mostly PrimeStakedXDC, which the protocol prices 1:1 as XDC without a market exchange-rate feed, and the price path itself runs through a single-reporter aggregator on a fifteen-minute delay. Economic control and exit both sit at the bottom of the card and the {{grade}} overall grade follows: one externally owned account owns the ProxyAdmin and can upgrade the token and adapter logic with no delay, and the primary exit is eligibility-gated. The design is a familiar CDP mechanism: mint against collateral, burn to repay, liquidate weak positions, and use a stability module for peg support, but the collateral base and chain liquidity make it materially riskier than larger Ethereum CDP systems.

dllr-sovryn.title: Rootstock's Mynt Basket
dllr-sovryn.text: DLLR is Sovryn's BTC-backed dollar on Rootstock, minted 1:1 through the Mynt aggregator against a basket of Rootstock {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoins that is almost entirely ZUSD with a trace of DOC, and the holder balances can be read on-chain. Underlying bAssets carry {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} against rBTC, so the backing pillar grades reasonably despite the concentration. The {{grade}} overall grade is set by the exit pillar, the weakest of the three: Mynt {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} returns ZUSD or DOC rather than a same-notional dollar, and Pharos has no comparable route to score. The residual risks are concentration in Rootstock liquidity, Sovryn governance, and the quality of the underlying BTC-backed stablecoins, plus a Sovryn timelock that can appoint a manager able to burn any holder's balance; opaque {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} is not among them.

xusd-babelfish.title: The Rootstock Stablecoin Basket
xusd-babelfish.text: XUSD is BabelFish's Rootstock basket stablecoin, minted 1:1 from accepted {{term:bridge}}bridged{{/term}} stablecoins and redeemed into them through a basket-level {{term:psm}}PSM-style{{/term}} module with balancing fees. Pharos tracks live branch balances directly from the basket holder: at the reviewed capture the basket was about nine-tenths Sovryn DLLR, with bridged USDT for most of the rest and a sliver of Money on Chain DOC, while the admissible USDC and DAI variants held no balance. The model is useful but recursive: XUSD inherits the risks of Rootstock {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}} liquidity, DLLR's own basket, and BabelFish's balancing fees. Two control facts sit under the card: the masset manager that owns the token can burn any holder's balance without an allowance check, and its documented custody chain accounts for only about half of the supply-backing balances, with the rest unlocated. Exit is the weakest of the three pillars. XUSD offers a basket exit route with recursive dependency risk, and no fiat issuer stands behind it.

susdd-tron-dao-reserve.title: Savings USDD Wrapper
susdd-tron-dao-reserve.text: sUSDD is a savings wrapper over USDD, so the first analytical move is to look through it rather than invent a new peg mechanism. Users deposit USDD, receive a wrapper whose exchange rate appreciates, and ultimately inherit USDD's reserve, PSM, and redemption assumptions on the way out. The wrapper contract itself is comparatively clean, with immutable DSR-style mechanics and no owner or proxy, but the base asset below it is still the load-bearing risk. Pharos records self-reported real-time USDD data, which is useful without being independent reserve assurance. The card shows the split directly: the wrapper's own exit and control pillars score high, yet the {{grade}} overall grade is capped at the parent USDD score, so sUSDD cannot rate above the coin it wraps.

onyc-onre.title: The Reinsurance NAV Token
onyc-onre.text: ONYC is a Solana NAV token tied to OnRe-managed structured insurance and reinsurance yield rather than a par-value payment stablecoin with cash in a bank account. Its value is meant to accrue from insurance-market collateral returns, with monthly Apex agreed-upon-procedures NAV statements and OnRe's Bermuda segregated-account licensing providing the institutional wrapper. The reserve picture is more conventional than the reinsurance label suggests: OnRe's August 2026 schedule of assets puts roughly half the collateral in short-term Treasury bills and about a quarter in USDG, with the remainder spread across sUSDS, syrupUSDC, sUSDe, Kamino lending positions, USDC, and cash, while the bound reinsurance contracts sit on top as contingent obligations rather than extra assets. Primary access remains governed by OnRe's platform terms, and the mint surface runs through an upgradeable Solana program controlled by a 3-of-6 multisig with no delay. The {{grade}} overall grade is set by the exit pillar, the weakest of the three: every redemption still depends on an eligibility-gated, high-touch issuer process, and the product is under two years old.

sources.label: OnRe Transparency Hub (Schedule of Assets, snapshot 2026-08-14)

apyusd-apyx.title: Apyx Savings Share
apyusd-apyx.text: apyUSD is a savings wrapper over apxUSD that turns Apyx's preferred-share collateral into a rising NAV. It is not a cash layer. The parent reserve stack is the interesting part: Digital Asset Treasury preferred equity and liquidity buffers sit underneath, which is a long way from a plain Treasury-bill stablecoin. In June 2026 that collateral thesis got its real-work moment and failed it: apxUSD followed Strategy's preferred stock below par and still trades under the dollar, so the wrapper's card is mostly inherited arithmetic: an ERC-4626 share can compound yield all it likes, but it compounds on top of whatever the parent is actually worth. Pharos reads the wrapper's holdings straight from the ERC-4626 vault while still carrying the parent dependency forward: a child cannot rate above its required parent, so the {{grade}} overall grade is the parent's ceiling, and backing is the weakest of the three pillars even though the wrapper's own exit and economic-control lines grade well above it. A savings share is only as good as the thing being saved.

susd1plus-lorenzo.title: Lorenzo Strategy Dollar
susd1plus-lorenzo.text: sUSD1+ is Lorenzo's staked receipt over the USD1+ strategy dollar, blending WLFI USD1 reserve yield with delta-neutral CEX strategies on BNB Chain. The wrapper is {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}}, with returns sourced from {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}} {{term:basis-trade}}basis trade{{/term}} positions and CEX strategy access driven by {{term:funding-rate}}funding rate{{/term}} dynamics. Public data supports metadata and supply tracking, but the reserve and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} mechanics are less transparent than the cleaner ERC-4626 wrappers, so the entry carries exotic collateral and CEX-strategy {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} risk. Lorenzo publishes no weights for the USD1, USDT, and USDC inputs or the RWA, CeFi, and DeFi sleeves, and no exchange margin or liquidation data. Economic control is the weakest of the three pillars: a 2-of-3 Safe holds the vault manager's admin and operator roles and can replace the upgradeable logic without delay. The {{grade}} overall grade is also capped at the parent USD1 score, so the wrapper cannot rate above the dollar it settles into. Withdrawals follow a seven-day minimum hold and a biweekly settlement cycle.

savusd-avant.title: Avant Staked Dollar
savusd-avant.text: savUSD is Avant's staked avUSD receipt, with the exchange rate rising as the senior tranche earns from actively managed market-neutral strategies. The protection stack is explicit but not magical: Avant points to a Reserve Fund and junior avUSDx tranche before savUSD takes losses, while Pennyworks supplies the weekly NAV calculation. Unstaking has a one-day cooldown with no yield, and the final exit still inherits avUSD's 1:1 USDC redemption process. Pharos therefore reads savUSD as a yield sleeve over a managed strategy book, not as a faster or safer dollar than its parent.

steakusdc-steakhouse.title: Circle, With Borrowers
steakusdc-steakhouse.text: Steakhouse USDC is an immutable MetaMorpho vault share over USDC, so the base dollar is Circle's but the yield comes from borrowers in Steakhouse-curated Morpho markets. The vault leaves Circle's reserve story unchanged and adds curator choices, lending collateral, and withdrawal liquidity on top of it. Pharos treats the wrapper minting as deposit-only share accounting while inheriting the underlying USDC issuer risk and tracking the Steakhouse governance surface separately. That governance surface is what holds the {{grade}} overall grade: the vault's supervisor sits behind a Steakhouse Safe shared with another tracked Steakhouse vault, and the card is capped for that concentration despite strong pillar scores. It is a clean USDC yield wrapper, but exits still depend on available Morpho liquidity, and the control address is the same one its sibling vault answers to.

bbqusdc-steakhouse.title: Smokehouse's Higher-Risk USDC Vault
bbqusdc-steakhouse.text: Smokehouse USDC is Steakhouse's high-yield MetaMorpho vault over USDC, built for borrowers and collateral types that sit outside the calmer Prime line. The wrapper itself uses a clear mechanism: an immutable ERC-4626 vault with no proxy, shares minted only against USDC deposits, and a Steakhouse Safe that can steer allocations and fees but cannot conjure base dollars or block a holder's transfer. That structure is why the {{grade}} overall grade sits at the ceiling set by its USDC parent: a child cannot rate above the asset it wraps, so the vault inherits Circle's reserve quality on the backing line and Circle's blacklist on the freeze line, while its own exit pillar leads the card because shares redeem against whatever USDC liquidity the Morpho markets hold. Economic control is the weakest of the three pillars, though only narrowly. The residual risk is the one the name advertises: exotic collateral, a curator who chooses it, and an exit that depends on Morpho markets unwinding faster than depositors change their minds.

srusde-strata.title: Strata's Senior USDe Tranche
srusde-strata.text: srUSDe is Strata's senior ERC-4626 tranche over a strategy that stakes USDe into Ethena's yield stack, with jrUSDe taking first-loss before senior holders are touched. The tranche structure gives senior capital a subordination buffer and a benchmark-rate yield floor. The discipline argument aged badly in July 2026, when Lido's EarnUSD vault began allocating to PT-srUSDe, the fixed-rate claim on this very tranche, looped on Aave with leverage extended through Twyne. The naked leveraged loop that tranching was supposed to replace has simply been rebuilt one layer up, with the senior tranche as its collateral. It is still not a plain dollar: exits depend on Strata tranche liquidity and settlement rules rather than 1:1 issuer redemption, which is why exit is the weakest of the three pillars and the main drag on the {{grade}} overall grade despite a respectable backing score. The senior wrapper still inherits Ethena's liquid-stablecoin, BTC, ETH/LST, CEX-hedge, and custody assumptions; the junior tranche absorbs the first loss, and a junior-exhausting event can still impair senior principal.

sources.label: CryptoBriefing: EarnUSD strategy loops PT-srUSDe on Aave via Twyne (July 22, 2026)

syzusd-yuzu.title: Yuzu Staked Wrapper
syzusd-yuzu.text: syzUSD is the staked wrapper for Yuzu USD, so its dollar story begins one layer below the token you are looking at. The wrapper appreciates against yzUSD as curated DeFi strategies accrue yield, while exits inherit Yuzu's KYC-gated redemption and liquidity-buffer constraints. Accountable's real-time reserve feed is the right transparency surface, but Pharos keeps the wrapper identity separate so the same underlying risk is not counted twice as fresh backing. That distinction matters because syzUSD holders are taking strategy-vault risk, parent-coin risk, and young-chain deployment risk in one receipt: Plasma is the only native issuance route, and the Ethereum, Monad, HyperEVM, Sei, Pharos, and Berachain units are Chainlink CCIP representations administered by Yuzu. The wrapper's own pillars are scored, with exit the strongest line and backing the weakest, but the overall card reads not rated because the parent yzUSD cannot currently be rated on the evidence reviewed. Until the parent clears that bar, no wrapper grade can exist above it.

fxsave-f-x-protocol.title: f(x) Stability Vault
fxsave-f-x-protocol.text: fxSAVE is an auto-compounding ERC-4626 receipt over f(x) Protocol's Stability Pool, so a deposit is a strategy position from the first block. The exit path runs through fxSP into a fxUSD-and-USDC mix, then onward into fxUSD's CDP machinery backed by WBTC and wstETH. That gives holders strategy yield and peg-support exposure in one package, but it also imports oracle, liquidation, Curve-pool, and governance-tuned collateral risk. Pharos classifies it as a strategy-vault variant of fxUSD, so its {{grade}} overall grade cannot exceed its parent's, and the exit pillar is the weakest line on its card because every route out shares the same fxUSD failure domain. The wrapper may look like savings, while the engine underneath is still a leveraged crypto collateral system with better manners.

steakusdt-steakhouse.title: Steakhouse USDT Lending Vault
steakusdt-steakhouse.text: Steakhouse USDT is a MetaMorpho vault share over USDT; yield comes from borrower interest in Steakhouse-curated lending markets. The trust stack is Tether first, Morpho market liquidity second, and Steakhouse curator discipline third. Pharos keeps the Tether issuer and blacklist dependency attached while separately treating the wrapper as a lending vault whose withdrawals rely on available USDT liquidity or returning market capacity. Backing is the weakest of the three pillars because the Tether reserve is inherited, and the {{grade}} overall grade is held by a cap on the Steakhouse control Safe shared with another tracked vault. It is a usable yield sleeve rather than a redemption backstop: the exit runs through Morpho liquidity and the base dollar is still Tether's.

susn-noon.title: Noon's Yield Receipt
susn-noon.text: sUSN is the staked savings form of Noon USN, so its NAV appreciates while base USN remains the non-yielding settlement token. The wrapper inherits a reserve mix that is far busier than the name suggests: private credit, CLO exposure, DeFi lending, principal tokens, and a small Treasury-bill sleeve, with Accountable providing a real-time proof feed. That makes sUSN a yield receipt over a credit portfolio, with no clean par redemption promise of its own. Pharos tracks it separately because wrapper supply, NAV, and liquidity can diverge from liquid USN even though final exits still route through Noon whitelisting and USN reserve constraints. The canonical Ethereum vault carries a per-account blacklist under a Noon admin Safe, and the zkSync, Sophon, and Starknet deployments are Hyperlane representations of that same locked inventory. Backing is the weakest of the three pillars, and the {{grade}} overall grade is capped at the parent USN score: the wrapper accounting is transparent, but every door between savings yield and cash belongs to Noon.

mre7yield-midas.title: Midas Re7 Yield Token
mre7yield-midas.text: mRe7YIELD is a Midas and Re7 Capital liquid-yield token, with NAV appreciation sourced from DeFi lending, liquidity provision, restaking, funding-rate trades, and options strategies. That mix may be institutionally packaged, but it is not a cash reserve and should not be read as one. Pharos gives credit for the Midas transparency feed while flagging the missing position-level strategy composition, the unpublished margin and liquidation disclosures, and the concentrated Midas mint and admin surface. The {{grade}} overall grade reflects an exit pillar that is the weakest of the three, with primary redemption gated to eligible holders through Midas rails and backing scored on an undisclosed position book. It is a managed strategy note; the durable constraint is that neither the positions nor the exit capacity is published.

hbusdt-hyperbeat.title: Hyperbeat USDT Vault
hbusdt-hyperbeat.text: hbUSDT is Hyperbeat's {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} vault share on HyperEVM over USDT strategy exposure, built on Midas vault contracts and accepting USDT0 as the enabled deposit token. Pharos records the reserve as one dynamic strategy envelope rather than a fixed split: Hyperbeat's documentation describes automated deployment of deposits into HyperEVM lending and strategy protocols under RockawayX risk oversight, but publishes no constituent or venue weights. The Accountable proof-of-solvency dashboard that is supposed to supply live visibility returned server errors on every check across July and August 2026, so the claimed real-time feed is not retrievable and the whole book is scored as known-unknown. The {{grade}} overall grade sits below its USDT parent ceiling, and the exit pillar is the weakest of the three. The parent leg inherits Tether's redemption discretion and USDT0's cross-chain settlement assumptions; the wrapper adds Hyperbeat vault liquidity, strategy allocation, and single-chain HyperEVM execution risk. Minting is open to any depositor with no cap set, while a single Midas key can grant the mint role and a two-day timelock guards upgrades. It is yield-bearing because more machinery sits between the holder and the dollar, and the durable constraint is that none of that machinery is independently reconciled.

witry-brix.title: Wrapped Turkish Lira Yield
witry-brix.text: wiTRY is Brix's ERC-4626 staking wrapper over iTRY, a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} claim that accrues fund yield against a token backed by shares of the Digital Liquidity Fund, a regulated basket of Turkish-lira money-market funds. The Ethereum wrapper can be verified on-chain, and Brix's Accountable dashboard publishes a signed assets-and-liabilities snapshot showing reserves matching supply. What it does not show is the fund look-through: the underlying money-market funds, their weights, and their maturities stay undisclosed, so Pharos treats the position as {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} collateral with high jurisdictional and operational risk for a thinly traded TRY product. Exit runs through a cooldown unstake or a fee-bearing fast {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} into iTRY, with final lira exposure inheriting the iTRY issuer and its Zodia Custody arrangement. Pharos publishes no research rating for wiTRY: the track record is under six months, no reviewed same-notional exit route exists, and the critical evidence is classed as insufficient.

sources.label: Brix iTRY backing and custody documentation

srusd-reservoir.title: Reservoir Savings Token
srusd-reservoir.text: srUSD is Reservoir's savings wrapper over rUSD, so the immediate asset is a yield-accruing share and the underlying risk is the Reservoir balance sheet. That balance sheet is a mixed book: stablecoin PSM liquidity, RWA allocations, Morpho and Euler lending vaults, and governance-approved credit strategies. The wrapper is minted by burning rUSD and redeemed by minting it back, so it adds exchange-rate and exit-to-rUSD mechanics while rUSD itself still depends on PSM liquidity and protocol risk controls for the actual stablecoin exit. Reservoir's real-time reserve endpoint gives Pharos a live window into that stack. Backing is the weakest of the three pillars, and the {{grade}} overall grade is capped at the parent rUSD rating.

usdn-smardex.title: Delta-Neutral USDN
usdn-smardex.text: SMARDEX USDN is an Ethereum synthetic dollar built around a wstETH-backed vault and delta-neutral protocol mechanics, unrelated to Noble's USDN despite the shared ticker. Users mint and redeem through the vault, but the process can be throttled by protocol imbalance and a two-step oracle validation flow, so the peg mechanism is more state machine than cashier window. The token also rebases, which turns yield into a protocol accounting event rather than a separate savings wrapper. The {{grade}} overall grade turns on economic control, the weakest of the three pillars: the protocol proxy is USDN's sole minter and rebaser, and its 2-of-3 governance Safe can grant the upgrade role and replace the implementation immediately, because elegant delta-neutral math still needs someone to hold the keys.

scusd-rings.title: Rings Stable Collateral
scusd-rings.text: Rings scUSD is the liquid scAsset, distinct from the stkscUSD savings wrapper that carries the advertised yield, so any yield figure belongs to a different token. The collateral model accepts stablecoins and routes a strategy sleeve through Trevee/Veda BoringVault infrastructure into venues such as Aave and Morpho, so the backing is part cash-like collateral and part curated DeFi exposure. Proof is still self-reported through published backing addresses, with Pharos carrying an explicit notice that deeper on-chain reserve tracking is pending, and no dated split by stablecoin or strategy exists. The governance path runs through the Veda/Paladin Safe, timelock, RolesAuthority, and Teller machinery, which is orderly enough to document and centralized enough to matter. On the card, economic control leads while backing and exit are the two weak pillars, which is what holds the {{grade}} overall grade down.

weusd-picwe.title: PicWe's Disputed Dollar Wrapper
weusd-picwe.text: WEUSD is PicWe's omni-chain dollar token, minted and redeemed through PicWe-operated contracts on BSC, Base, Arbitrum, Plume, and Movement. The backing claim is the problem. PicWe's current documentation describes 1:1 USDC mint and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}, earlier PicWe materials describe a basket of roughly nine USDT to one MOVE, and no attestation or itemized reserve inventory reconciles either story. Pharos' July 2026 contract reads deepen the doubt: the EVM mint contract held under one USDC against tens of thousands of WEUSD outstanding, and the Movement package that carries most of the supply stores dual MOVE and stablecoin reserve counters far below circulating supply. Pharos therefore treats the composition as a single unresolved envelope rather than a USDC link. Mint authority is uncapped and held by a PicWe admin key, which is why economic control is the weakest of the three pillars behind the {{grade}} overall grade. The durable constraint is a backing claim that no published evidence reconciles.

gbpe-monerium.title: GBP E-Money Rail
gbpe-monerium.text: GBPe is Monerium's British-pound e-money token, issued under an Icelandic EMI licence and now authorized as an EMT under MiCA, with mint and burn handled through KYC'd bank-transfer rails. The reserve story is meant to be dull: safeguarded GBP client funds and permitted EMI reserve assets, with e-money holders holding a statutory priority claim under Icelandic bankruptcy law. The {{grade}} overall grade reflects how little of that dullness is documented. Monerium publishes only entity-wide audited totals and says public attestations are still being prepared, so no GBPe-specific safeguarded-assets-to-liabilities reconciliation or asset split exists for Pharos to score. Backing and exit are the two weakest pillars, while economic control, with three chain-local 3-of-6 Safes over six issuer-native deployments, is the strongest line on the card. Primary redemption runs only through Monerium's onboarding, which the card scores as eligibility-gated. For a non-USD stablecoin, that bank-rail dependence is both the product and the risk, and the constraint is disclosure: a regulated claim that the public record cannot yet reconcile.

qcad-stablecorp.title: Regulated CAD Stablecoin
qcad-stablecorp.text: QCAD is a Canadian-dollar stablecoin with the sort of regulatory scaffolding most small fiat tokens can only gesture at: FINTRAC registration, the QCAD Digital Trust framework, and CAD reserves held 1:1 at regulated Canadian institutions.
